Step 0. What and why

This step gives the business problem, the question for leadership and the method that answers it with past transactions. Each later step answers one part of the question.

Purpose. This step answers: what must a new fraud policy do for the business, and how can we test it before a real launch? It supports this decision: approve a challenger policy for a champion/challenger test.

0a. The business problem

Situation. An online merchant accepts card payments. The policy gives one of three actions to each transaction: approve, review or decline. A review sends the transaction to an analyst before the approval. A set of static rules selects the action. This rule set is the current policy: the champion.

Complication. The fraud loss goes up. Stricter rules decline more good customers, and a false decline also costs money: lost margin and customer friction. The analyst team can examine only 120 alerts each day (as-03). Fraud patterns change over time, so static rules lose value.

Question. Which policy gives the lowest total cost of fraud loss, false declines and reviews, with the same review capacity?

Resolution. Build a fraud score with a model. Put each transaction in a tier by its expected cost in dollars, inside the review capacity. Compare this challenger with the champion on the same past transactions. Give fraud operations readable rules for the decline tier. Retrain the score each month and monitor the drift.

If the challenger wins on the past transactions, test it on 10% of real transactions before a full rollout.

Decision that this notebook supports. Approve the challenger policy for a champion/challenger test on 10% of transactions.

Success metric. The total cost each month at the same review capacity. Guardrail metric: the decline rate of good transactions. Its limit is 3% (as-08).

0b. Method and data strategy

A technical reader asks one question first. How can we compare two policies without a live test?

The data has the fraud label of each past transaction. Thus we know the actual cost of each action on each transaction. An approved fraud transaction costs its amount. A declined good transaction costs lost margin and customer friction. We use an offline replay in four moves:

  1. Build the champion. The data does not give the rules of the merchant. Thus we build a champion ourselves (assumption as-06): a decision tree with three levels on month 1. It does not change after month 1, like static rules.
  2. Build the challenger. A model gives a fraud score from the data of months 1–3. The policy ranks each transaction by its expected cost in dollars.
  3. Set both policies on the same month. Both policies set their thresholds on month 4. They use the same three tiers, the same costs and the same review capacity.
  4. Replay both policies on months 5–6. Each policy gives an action to each test transaction. The fraud label gives the actual cost of each action. We compare the total cost each month.

The replay keeps all conditions the same, except the score and the value that ranks the transactions. Thus a difference in the total cost comes from the policy, not from the data or the costs.

The champion is our assumption, not the real rules of the merchant. A reader must know this before any result. Each gain in this notebook is a gain against a champion that we built.

Question Answer
What does a real merchant have? A production rule set and an analyst team. In a real project, these rules are the champion, and this section is not necessary.
What does the data not give? Vesta published the transactions and the fraud labels. It did not publish the rules of the merchant, or the action of the merchant on each transaction.
What do we build? A decision tree with three levels, fit on month 1 (as-06). It gives at most eight rule segments, like a small rule set. The fraud rate of a segment is the champion score. Inside a segment, the analysts review the largest amounts first. The tree does not change after month 1, like static rules.
Why this choice? Many merchants start with a small static rule set. A tree gives such rules from the data, with no hand-made thresholds. The champion uses the same three tiers, costs and review capacity as the challenger (as-03).
Which assumptions go with it? as-06: the champion rules. as-03: the review capacity. as-01, as-02, as-05: the costs. as-08: the guardrail limit.
How can it be wrong? Real rules can be stronger: more segments, data from more months, regular updates, or a vendor score. Then the gain of the challenger is smaller. Real rules can also be weaker, but we do not assume that.
How do we test it? Step 6d repeats branch 4 against a ladder of four champions, from our static rules to the same GBM with thresholds on the fraud score. Step 6d gives the gain against each champion.
What does not depend on it? Three comparisons use the same GBM on both sides. The first is the dollar order against the score order (Step 5d). The others are three tiers against two tiers (Step 5c) and the monthly retrain (Part 2).
What does it mean for the claim? The headline gain is the upper end of a range. The lower end, against the strongest champion, is the gain that we can defend. The champion/challenger test of Step 7c measures the gain against the real rules.

Why months. The model scores future transactions in production. A split by time gives the same condition: the model never sees the months that test it. A month is also the unit of the business decisions: the cost each month and the retrain each month.

A random split puts transactions of the same customer in the training set and in the test set. Then the label after a chargeback (as-07) copies into the test, and the result is too good. Step 3b shows the size of this effect.

The limits of the method.

  • The replay does not see the effect of an action on later transactions. In production, a decline can stop a fraudster or lose a good customer.
  • The data has no chargeback dates. The replay assumes that all labels are complete when the model trains.
  • The costs are assumptions (as-01 to as-05). Step 7b repeats the result for other costs.
  • The champion is an assumption (as-06). The gain of the challenger depends on it (see the block above).
  • The data has no customer ID. The customer key uid is a proxy (Step 2).
  • The data is a sample of the payment flow of one merchant. The dollar values are for this sample.

Technical note. The replay has these parts. Each later step gives the code.

  • Actual cost. A transaction has the amount \(a\) and the fraud label \(y\). An approval costs \(y \cdot a \cdot L\). A decline costs \((1-y)(m \cdot a + f)\). A review costs \(y \cdot a \cdot L (1-q) + (1-y) f_r\). Step 5b defines the symbols and gives the expected cost.
  • Champion score. The fraud rate of the leaf of the tree. A small term from the rank of the amount puts the larger amounts first inside a leaf.
  • Champion thresholds. A grid search on month 4 finds the decline threshold with the lowest total cost. The review tier takes the next highest scores, up to the capacity.
  • Challenger score. A GBM on months 1–3, with a recalibration on month 4 (Step 5a). The policy gives each transaction the action with the lowest expected cost. The review tier takes the transactions where a review decreases the expected cost most.
  • Same review capacity. A real-time decision cannot wait for the end of the day. Thus each policy uses a threshold, not a daily rank. The code sets the threshold on month 4, so that the mean number of alerts each day equals the capacity.
  • Test months. No threshold and no model uses months 5–6. They give only the final result.

0c. How the notebook answers the question

Each step answers one part of the question:

  • Step 1. Which data gives the fraud label of each transaction, and what does it contain?
  • Step 2. How do we put the transactions in time order, and which features can the model use fairly? What does fraud cost if the merchant approves all transactions?
  • Step 3. Which rules must the challenger pass, and which months test it? What does the champion do on these months?
  • Step 4. Which columns and which model type put the fraud transactions first? How do we handle the low fraud rate?
  • Step 5. How does the score become an action: approve, review or decline?
  • Step 6. Does the challenger pass each rule? Is it better than the champion in dollars?
  • Step 7. What is the value of one more analyst, and how do we test the policy with real transactions?
  • Part 2. Does the score stay good over time, and how often do we retrain it?

Business note. The question is a trade between fraud loss and false declines, inside a fixed review capacity. The replay compares the two policies on actual labels, so each cost is a fact of the past under the cost assumptions. Step 1 shows the data that gives these labels.

Step 1. Get data

Step 0 set the question and the method: replay two policies on labeled past transactions at the same review capacity. This step answers: which data gives these labels, and what does it contain?

Purpose. This step gets the data and its meaning. It supports this decision: if the data can answer the business question.

1a. Why this data

The data is the IEEE-CIS Fraud Detection dataset of Vesta Corporation. Source: Kaggle competition ieee-fraud-detection, files train_transaction.csv and train_identity.csv. The two files use TransactionID as the key. The data is a fair proxy for the fraud decision of a card issuer or a merchant, for four reasons:

  • Real card-not-present payments. The transactions come from real e-commerce payments. Card-not-present fraud is the largest type of card fraud online.
  • The same data at the decision. Each transaction has the amount, the product, the card, the address, the email and the device. A fraud system has the same data at the time of the payment.
  • A fraud label for each transaction. The label comes from chargebacks. Thus we can calculate the actual cost of each action on each transaction.
  • Time order. TransactionDT gives the time of each transaction. Thus we can split the data by month and replay each month.

The data cannot show these things:

What the data does not show Why it matters What the notebook does
A customer ID History features need a customer key. A proxy key uid from the card, the address and the first day of the card (Step 2).
The meaning of most columns Vesta masked most columns. A reason code from a masked column has little meaning. A surrogate tree with readable features (Step 6).
The chargeback dates We do not know when each label becomes available. The retrain plan trains on all months except the last one when the labels are late (Part 2).
The rules and the actions of the merchant We do not know the real champion. A champion from a decision tree on month 1 (as-06, Step 0b).
The result of a different action A declined fraudster can come back. A declined good customer can leave. A live test on real transactions (Step 7).
The full payment flow The dollar values are for a sample. Scale the result with the actual volume.

1b. Key variables

The table gives the column groups that the story uses. The target is isFraud. Appendix A gives the meaning and the use of all columns of the two files.

Column group Columns Meaning in plain words Use
Label isFraud 1 = fraud. The label comes from a chargeback. It also marks later transactions of the same customer (as-07). Target
Time TransactionDT Seconds from a reference time. It is not a calendar date. Time order, day, month and hour (Step 2). Not a feature.
Amount TransactionAmt The amount of the payment in US dollars. Feature. Base of all dollar costs.
Product ProductCD The product code of the transaction (masked). Feature
Card card1–card6 Card data: for example the card network (card4) and debit or credit (card6). Vesta masked the other values. Feature. card1 is a part of uid.
Address and distance addr1, addr2, dist1, dist2 Billing region and country, and two distances (masked). Feature. addr1 is a part of uid.
Email P_emaildomain, R_emaildomain The email domain of the buyer and of the recipient. Feature. Step 2 adds email_match.
Counts C1–C14 Counts, for example the number of addresses for the card (masked). Feature
Time differences D1–D15 Days between events. D1 is the age of the card in days. Feature. D1 gives the first day of the card for uid.
Match flags M1–M9 Matches, for example the name on the card against the address (masked). Feature
Vesta features V1–V339 Features from Vesta: ranks, counts and other relations (masked). Feature. Step 1c keeps a part of them.
Identity DeviceType, DeviceInfo, id_30, id_31, id_33 The device, the system of the device, the browser and the screen. Only a part of the transactions has these values. Feature. Step 1c adds the flag has_identity.

A column with “Not a feature” never goes to the model. A masked column can be a feature, but it cannot give a readable reason for a decline.

1c. Load the data and look at it

The code joins the two files with SQL (DuckDB). The first run reads the two CSV files one time and writes a small Parquet copy. Later runs read the copy in a few seconds.

The V features come in groups with the same pattern of missing values. Two features of one group often carry the same information. To keep the model small, the code keeps two features of each group: the two with the most distinct values. This rule uses no label, so it does not cause leakage. Step 4a gives all column decisions.

The key parameters of the load are:

  • Features of each missing pattern of V: two, with the most distinct values.
  • Identity columns: DeviceType, DeviceInfo, id_30, id_31 and id_33.
  • Join: a left join, so each transaction stays in the data. The flag has_identity marks a transaction with identity data.
Load: join the two files with SQL (DuckDB) and keep the V features. The first run writes a Parquet file. 
# Purpose: Join the transaction file and the identity file with SQL (DuckDB). Keep two V features of each
#          missing pattern. Keep a Parquet copy for fast reloads.
# Input:   data/raw/train_transaction.csv, data/raw/train_identity.csv (first run only).
# Output:  `txn` (one row for each transaction), `V_KEEP` (V features that the code keeps),
#          `BASE_COLS`, `ID_COLS` (the other columns that the code reads).

BASE_COLS = (
    ["TransactionID", "isFraud", "TransactionDT", "TransactionAmt", "ProductCD"]
    + [f"card{i}" for i in range(1, 7)] + ["addr1", "addr2", "dist1", "dist2",
       "P_emaildomain", "R_emaildomain"]
    + [f"C{i}" for i in range(1, 15)] + [f"D{i}" for i in range(1, 16)]
    + [f"M{i}" for i in range(1, 10)]
)
ID_COLS = ["DeviceType", "DeviceInfo", "id_30", "id_31", "id_33"]

# First run only: read the two CSV files and write one Parquet file.
if not INTERIM_FILE.exists():
    INTERIM_FILE.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    con = duckdb.connect()
    con.sql(f"""CREATE VIEW t AS SELECT * FROM read_csv('{RAW_TXN.as_posix()}',
                header = true, sample_size = -1)""")
    con.sql(f"""CREATE VIEW i AS SELECT * FROM read_csv('{RAW_ID.as_posix()}',
                header = true, sample_size = -1)""")
    # V features: count the values and the distinct values of each column.
    v_cols = [c for c in con.sql("DESCRIBE t").df()["column_name"] if c.startswith("V")]
    stats = con.sql("SELECT " + ", ".join(
        f"COUNT({c}) AS n_{c}, approx_count_distinct({c}) AS d_{c}" for c in v_cols
    ) + " FROM t").df().iloc[0]
    vstat = pd.DataFrame({"col": v_cols,
                          "non_null": [stats[f"n_{c}"] for c in v_cols],
                          "distinct": [stats[f"d_{c}"] for c in v_cols]})
    # The same count of values = the same missing pattern. Keep the two columns with the most distinct values.
    v_keep = (vstat.sort_values("distinct", ascending=False)
              .groupby("non_null").head(2)["col"].tolist())
    select = ", ".join([f"t.{c}" for c in BASE_COLS + v_keep]
                       + [f"i.{c}" for c in ID_COLS]
                       + ["i.TransactionID IS NOT NULL AS has_identity"])
    # Left join: each transaction stays, with or without identity data.
    con.sql(f"""
        COPY (SELECT {select} FROM t LEFT JOIN i ON t.TransactionID = i.TransactionID)
        TO '{INTERIM_FILE.as_posix()}' (FORMAT parquet)
    """)

# Later runs: read the Parquet file (a few seconds).
txn = duckdb.sql(f"SELECT * FROM read_parquet('{INTERIM_FILE.as_posix()}')").df()
V_KEEP = [c for c in txn.columns if c.startswith("V")]
print(f"Transactions: {len(txn):,} | V features kept: {len(V_KEEP)} of 339")
Transactions: 590,540 | V features kept: 30 of 339

#          table of the initial state (printed), table of missing values by column group.

# Column groups of Step 1b. The V group holds only the V features that the load keeps.
col_groups = {
    "Label": ["isFraud"],
    "Time": ["TransactionDT"],
    "Amount": ["TransactionAmt"],
    "Product": ["ProductCD"],
    "Card": [f"card{i}" for i in range(1, 7)],
    "Address and distance": ["addr1", "addr2", "dist1", "dist2"],
    "Email": ["P_emaildomain", "R_emaildomain"],
    "Counts": [f"C{i}" for i in range(1, 15)],
    "Time differences": [f"D{i}" for i in range(1, 16)],
    "Match flags": [f"M{i}" for i in range(1, 10)],
    "Vesta features (kept)": V_KEEP,

}
MISS_CUT = 0.5  # A column with more missing values than this share counts as "mostly missing"
miss = pd.DataFrame([
    {"Column group": g, "Columns": len(cols),
     "Share missing": txn[cols].isna().to_numpy().mean(),

    for g, cols in col_groups.items()

# Size of the raw files: only the header line, so no full read of the CSV files.
raw_cols = {f: len(pd.read_csv(f, nrows=0).columns) if f.exists() else None for f in [RAW_TXN, RAW_ID]}
days = txn["TransactionDT"] / 86400  # TransactionDT is in seconds
feature_cols = [c for cols in col_groups.values() for c in cols]
N.update({
    "s1_rows": f"{len(txn):,}",
    "s1_cols": f"{txn.shape[1]}",
    "s1_raw_txn_cols": f"{raw_cols[RAW_TXN]}" if raw_cols[RAW_TXN] else "n/a",
    "s1_raw_id_cols": f"{raw_cols[RAW_ID]}" if raw_cols[RAW_ID] else "n/a",
    "s1_v_keep": f"{len(V_KEEP)}",
    "s1_day_first": f"{days.min():.0f}",
    "s1_day_last": f"{days.max():.0f}",
    "s1_days": f"{days.max() - days.min():.0f}",
    "s1_fraud_n": f"{int(txn['isFraud'].sum()):,}",
    "s1_fraud_rate": f"{txn['isFraud'].mean():.2%}",
    "s1_identity_share": f"{txn['has_identity'].mean():.0%}",
    "s1_miss_all": f"{txn[feature_cols].isna().to_numpy().mean():.0%}",
    "s1_miss_id": f"{miss.loc['Identity', 'Share missing']:.0%}",
    "s1_miss_v": f"{miss.loc['Vesta features (kept)', 'Share missing']:.0%}",
    "s1_miss_d": f"{miss.loc['Time differences', 'Share missing']:.0%}",
    "s1_cols_over_half": f"{int(miss['Columns with more than 50% missing'].sum())}",
    "s1_miss_cut": f"{MISS_CUT:.0%}",
})

# Initial state: one row for each fact.
state = pd.Series({
    "Rows (transactions)": N["s1_rows"],
    "Columns after the load": N["s1_cols"],
    "Columns in the raw files (transaction / identity)": f"{N['s1_raw_txn_cols']} / {N['s1_raw_id_cols']}",
    "V features kept": f"{N['s1_v_keep']} of 339",
    "Time range (days from the reference time)": f"{N['s1_day_first']} to {N['s1_day_last']}",
    "Fraud transactions": N["s1_fraud_n"],
    "Fraud rate": N["s1_fraud_rate"],
    "Transactions with identity data": N["s1_identity_share"],
    "Share missing, all columns": N["s1_miss_all"],
}, name="Value")
print(state.to_string())

The data has 590,540 transactions and 91 columns after the load. The raw files have 394 columns (transactions) and 41 columns (identity). The load keeps 30 of the V features. The data covers 182 days, from day 1 to day 183 after the reference time.

The data has 20,663 fraud transactions: a fraud rate of 3.50%. This rate is low, so a random score finds few fraud transactions. Step 3a explains why the notebook uses the PR-AUC for this reason. Step 4c examines the effect of the low rate on the training.

Missing values are frequent. Of all values, 38% are missing. Only 24% of the transactions have identity data, so the identity group has 81% missing values. The kept V features have 45% missing values, and the time differences have 58%. In total, 34 columns have more than 50% missing values. Step 2 explains why the GBM uses these values without a fill.

Business note. The data gives a fraud label, an amount and the data at the time of the payment for each transaction. Thus the replay can calculate the actual cost of each action. The data has no customer ID, no chargeback dates and few readable columns, and the notebook says where each limit matters. Step 2 puts the transactions in time order and builds the features that the model can use fairly.

Step 2. Clean and prepare data

Step 1 showed that the two Vesta files can answer the business question. They give the amount, the time and the fraud label of each transaction. But the data has no customer ID, the label of a customer can change after a chargeback, and many cells are empty. This step answers: which rows, which columns and which values can the model use, and what does fraud cost today?

Purpose. This step makes sure that the data can answer the business question without leakage. It supports this decision: the rows, the label and the features that the fraud score can use, and the baseline that the challenger must beat.

The data preparation follows one tree with three levels. Each level has one split axis. Each axis divides all cases into groups that do not overlap and that together cover all cases (MECE).

Level Split axis Groups What this data needs Section
Rows Is the record a valid transaction with a label? Not valid · valid Four technical checks. Then a time order and six months. 2a
Columns Does the business know the value at the time of the decision? Known before the decision · known only after the decision A customer key from earlier data. A label that can come from a later chargeback (as-07). A date that moves each month (D1n). 2b
Values Why is a cell empty or extreme? Structural · masked · extreme but real No imputation for the GBM. No cap on the amount. 2c

Then Step 2d makes new features from earlier transactions, and Step 2e measures the baseline: the fraud loss if the merchant approves all transactions.

2a. Rows: which transactions can the model learn from?

The first split asks if a record is a valid transaction. The code checks four conditions. A record is not valid if it repeats a transaction or if a key field is empty. It is also not valid if the amount is $0 or less, or if the label is not 0 or 1.

The data has no product or channel that is outside the business question. Thus each valid row is in scope.

Rows: four technical checks, then the time order, the day and the month of each transaction 
# Purpose: Check the rows, sort them by time and add `day`, `month` and `hour`.
# Input:   `txn` (from the load cell of Step 1).
# Output:  `txn` sorted by `TransactionDT`, with `day`, `month` and `hour`. Tables `row_checks` and `months`.

n_loaded = len(txn)
# Each check gives True for a row that is not valid.
row_checks = {
    "Duplicate TransactionID": txn["TransactionID"].duplicated(keep="first"),
    "Empty key field (ID, time, amount, label)": txn[
        ["TransactionID", "TransactionDT", "TransactionAmt", "isFraud"]].isna().any(axis=1),
    "Amount of $0 or less": txn["TransactionAmt"] <= 0,
    "Label not 0 or 1": ~txn["isFraud"].isin([0, 1]),
}
invalid = pd.concat(row_checks, axis=1).any(axis=1)
txn = txn[~invalid]

# Time order. A stable sort keeps the file order for two transactions in the same second.
txn = txn.sort_values("TransactionDT", kind="stable").reset_index(drop=True)
# TransactionDT counts seconds from a reference time that Vesta did not publish.
txn["day"] = (txn["TransactionDT"] // 86400).astype(int)
# Month = 30 days. The last 3 days go into month 6, so that no month has only a few days.
txn["month"] = np.minimum(txn["day"] // 30 + 1, 6).astype(int)
txn["hour"] = (txn["TransactionDT"] // 3600) % 24  # Hour of the reference clock, not local time

months = txn.groupby("month").agg(
    First_day=("day", "min"), Last_day=("day", "max"), Days=("day", "nunique"),
    Transactions=("isFraud", "size"), Fraud_rate=("isFraud", "mean"))
months.columns = ["First day", "Last day", "Days", "Transactions", "Fraud rate"]
N.update({
    "n_loaded": f"{n_loaded:,}", "n_invalid": f"{int(invalid.sum()):,}",
    "n_days": f"{txn['day'].nunique()}", "days_m6": f"{months.loc[6, 'Days']}",
    "days_m1": f"{months.loc[1, 'Days']}",
})
print(pd.Series({k: int(v.sum()) for k, v in row_checks.items()}, name="Rows that fail").to_string(), "\n")
fmt(months, {"Transactions": "{:,.0f}", "Fraud rate": "{:.2%}"})

0 of the 590,540 rows fail a check. The file is clean at the row level.

Time order and months. TransactionDT gives the seconds from a reference time. Vesta did not publish this time, so the data has no calendar date. The code sorts all rows by TransactionDT before any other step. Each feature that uses other transactions then can read only the earlier rows.

The data covers 182 days. The notebook calls each block of 30 days a month. Month 1 has 29 days, because the first day of the data is day 1. Month 6 has 33 days, because it also takes the last days of the data. Thus all results in dollars use a cost for each 30 days, not a cost for each calendar month.

2b. Columns: which values does the business know at the time of the decision?

A column can be a feature only if the business knows its value when the transaction arrives. Three columns of this data need a decision before Step 4: the customer key, the label and the first day of the card.

The customer key uid is a proxy. The data has no customer ID. Fraud is a behavior of a customer, so the history features need a key for the customer. A common key in the Kaggle discussion joins three values:

  • card1: a masked code of the card.
  • addr1: a masked code of the billing region.
  • D1n: the first day of the card. D1 gives the days from the start of the card to the transaction. Thus D1n = day − D1.

Two real customers can share a uid, and one customer can have two uid values. If D1 or addr1 is empty, the key is empty. The code measures these cases.

The label after a chargeback (as-07). Vesta gives a fraud label to the transaction with a chargeback. It also gives the label to the later transactions of the same account, email address or billing address. Thus a customer with one fraud often has more fraud labels after it. A feature that reads later transactions of the customer, or the labels of earlier transactions, can copy the label.

The data has no chargeback dates. Thus the code cannot know when the business learned about an earlier fraud.

The first day of the card D1n is a date. Each month brings new cards, so the values of D1n move up each month. A model that learns from a date does not repeat its result in later months. Thus D1n is part of the key, but not a feature. The model uses D1, the age of the card.

Customer key uid (a proxy), the label after a chargeback (as-07) and the drift of D1n 
# Purpose: Make the customer key `uid` and measure its weak points. Measure the effect of as-07.
# Input:   `txn`.
# Output:  `txn` with `D1n` and `uid`. Table `key_checks`. Numbers for the text.

txn["D1n"] = txn["day"] - txn["D1"]  # First day of the card. Only for the customer key.
txn["uid"] = (txn["card1"].astype(str) + "_" + txn["addr1"].astype(str)
              + "_" + txn["D1n"].astype(str))
key_ok = txn["D1"].notna() & txn["addr1"].notna()  # The key has all three parts

# as-07: did the same uid have an earlier fraud? Only for a description of the label. No feature uses it.
g = txn.groupby("uid", sort=False)
earlier_fraud = (g["isFraud"].cumsum() - txn["isFraud"]) > 0
size_uid = g["isFraud"].transform("size")
fraud = txn["isFraud"] == 1

key_checks = pd.Series({
    "Distinct uid values": txn["uid"].nunique(),
    "Transactions with an empty part of the key (D1 or addr1)": int((~key_ok).sum()),
    "Transactions of a uid with more than one transaction": int((size_uid > 1).sum()),
    "Fraud transactions after an earlier fraud of the same uid": int((fraud & earlier_fraud & key_ok).sum()),
}, name="Value")
N.update({
    "n_uid": f"{txn['uid'].nunique():,}",
    "key_empty": f"{(~key_ok).mean():.1%}",
    "uid_repeat": f"{(size_uid > 1).mean():.0%}",
    "fraud_after_fraud": f"{earlier_fraud[fraud & key_ok].mean():.0%}",
    "fr_after_fraud": f"{txn.loc[earlier_fraud & key_ok, 'isFraud'].mean():.0%}",
    "fr_no_earlier": f"{txn.loc[~earlier_fraud & key_ok, 'isFraud'].mean():.1%}",
    "d1n_med_1": f"{txn.loc[txn['month'] == 1, 'D1n'].median():.0f}",
    "d1n_med_6": f"{txn.loc[txn['month'] == 6, 'D1n'].median():.0f}",
})
del g, size_uid, earlier_fraud, fraud
key_checks.map("{:,.0f}".format).to_frame()

The key gives 199,070 customers. 69% of the transactions belong to a uid with more than one transaction, so a history exists for most transactions. For 11.3% of the transactions, a part of the key is empty. These transactions have no uid history, and the model uses only the card1 history for them.

The label after a chargeback has a large effect. 63% of the fraud transactions with a full key come after an earlier fraud of the same uid. After an earlier fraud, the fraud rate of a uid is 66%. Without an earlier fraud, it is 0.9%.

Thus a feature that knows the earlier labels of a customer looks strong in a test. In production, the business learns about a fraud only weeks later, from the chargeback. Step 4a compares the history features with this risk (the decision on history features).

The median of D1n goes from day 9 in month 1 to day 150 in month 6. This change comes from the calendar, not from the risk. Part 2 shows its drift.

2c. Values: missing values and extreme values

The split axis for an empty cell is the cause. Either the source of the value does not exist for this transaction (structural), or Vesta masked the meaning, so the cause is not known (masked). For an extreme value, the axis is reality: the value is impossible, or it is extreme but real.

Values: share of empty cells by column group, and the fraud rate with and without identity data 
# Purpose: Measure the empty cells by column group and show that an empty cell carries risk information.

    "Counts (C1–C14)": ([f"C{i}" for i in range(1, 15)], "Masked"),
    "Time deltas (D1–D15)": ([f"D{i}" for i in range(1, 16)], "Structural: no earlier event"),
    "Match flags (M1–M9)": ([f"M{i}" for i in range(1, 10)], "Masked"),

}
missing_groups = pd.DataFrame([
    {"Column group": name, "Columns": len(cols), "Cause": cause,
     "Mean share empty": txn[cols].isna().mean().mean(),
     "Highest share empty": txn[cols].isna().mean().max()}
    for name, (cols, cause) in GROUPS.items()]).set_index("Column group")

has_id = txn["has_identity"].astype(bool)
# The loaded columns, without the columns of Steps 2a and 2b.
loaded = [c for c in txn.columns if c not in {"day", "month", "hour", "D1n", "uid"}]
N.update({
    "miss_id_all": f"{txn['DeviceType'].isna().mean():.0%}",
    "miss_id_in": f"{txn.loc[has_id, 'DeviceType'].isna().mean():.1%}",

    "amt_med": f"${txn['TransactionAmt'].median():,.0f}",
    # Raw columns of the two files (header rows only). TransactionID is in both files.
    "n_raw_cols": (f"{len(pd.read_csv(RAW_TXN, nrows=0).columns) + len(pd.read_csv(RAW_ID, nrows=0).columns) - 1}"
                   if RAW_TXN.exists() and RAW_ID.exists() else "434"),
})

34 of the 91 loaded columns have more than 50% empty cells. What we do with each group:

Group Example in this data What we do
Structural missing value DeviceType is empty for 76% of all transactions, but for only 2.4% of the transactions with an identity row. The fraud rate is 7.8% with identity data and 2.1% without it. Keep the empty cell. The flag has_identity (Step 2d) also records the source.
Masked missing value A D column is empty for up to 93% of the transactions. Vesta does not say why. Keep the empty cell. The GBM learns the risk of the empty cells from the data.
Impossible value The row checks of Step 2a find no amount of $0 or less. No change is necessary.
Extreme but real value TransactionAmt goes up to $31,937. The 99th percentile is $1,104, and the median is $69. Keep the value. Do not cap it. A large amount is the largest fraud loss.

Why the GBM needs no imputation. An empty cell in this data often tells something about the risk. The identity data shows this: the fraud rate with identity data is different from the fraud rate without it. A median or a fixed value in the empty cell puts the transaction into a group of real values, and the model loses this information.

Technical note. The GBM (HistGradientBoostingClassifier) cuts each numeric feature into at most 255 bins at the quantiles of the training data. Empty cells go into a separate bin. At each split, the GBM sends the empty cells to the side that gives the better fit. Thus the GBM learns a risk for “empty” from the data, and it needs no imputation.

The GBM also uses only the order of the values. Thus an extreme amount goes into the top bin and does not change the other splits. A cap at the 99th percentile changes nothing for the GBM. The logistic regression of Step 4b cannot read an empty cell. It uses the median of the training data and adds a flag for each empty cell (SimpleImputer with add_indicator=True).

2d. Feature engineering

Feature engineering makes a better input from the raw columns. The split axis is the rows that a new feature reads. These rows are the same transaction only, the earlier transactions of the same key, or the later transactions of the same key. The table shows what this data needs in each group.

Group Method In this data
Same transaction: one column A change of scale or a part of a value hour from TransactionDT. log_amt = ln(1 + amount), for the logistic regression. cents: the part of the amount after the decimal point.
Same transaction: two columns A flag for a match email_match = 1 if the email domain of the buyer and of the recipient are the same.
Same transaction: two files A flag for the source has_identity = 1 if the transaction has a row in the identity file.
Earlier transactions of the same key History features Four features for uid and four for card1. They give the count of earlier transactions, the amount against their mean, the hours since the last one and the count today.
Later transactions of the same key History features over all transactions Not used. The business does not know the later transactions at the time of the decision, and they carry the label after a chargeback (as-07).

The history features show a change from the normal behavior of a customer. For example, a fraud often has an amount far above the earlier amounts of the card, or many transactions in one day.

Technical note. For transaction t of key k (uid or card1), with the rows in time order:

  • _n = the number of transactions of k before t.
  • _amt_ratio = amount(t) / mean amount of the transactions of k before t. The value is empty if k has no earlier transaction.
  • _hours_since = (TransactionDT(t) − TransactionDT of the last transaction of k before t) / 3,600.
  • _n_today = the number of transactions of k before t on the same day.

The code calculates each feature with a cumulative sum or a cumulative count in the sorted data, so each value uses only earlier rows. The argument past_only=False makes the leakage version over all transactions of k. Only the evidence of the decision on history features in Step 4a uses it.

The history starts at the first day of the data, so the counts grow over time. Part 2 shows this drift. In production, a history window of fixed length (for example 90 days) stops it.

Features: amount, match and source flags, history features from earlier transactions, feature lists 
# Purpose: Make the features of Step 2d and the feature lists for Steps 3 and 4.
# Input:   `txn` (sorted, with `day` and `uid`).
# Output:  `txn` with the new features. `add_history()`, `HIST`, `EXCLUDE`, `CAT_COLS`, `NUM_COLS`.
#          `train`, `valid`, `test` (the split of Step 3, dec-01).

# Same transaction.
txn["log_amt"] = np.log1p(txn["TransactionAmt"])
txn["cents"] = (txn["TransactionAmt"] % 1).round(3)
txn["email_match"] = (txn["P_emaildomain"] == txn["R_emaildomain"]).astype(float)
txn["has_identity"] = txn["has_identity"].astype(float)


def add_history(frame, key, prefix, past_only=True):
    """Return the frame with four history features for a key. past_only=False reads all transactions (leakage)."""
    g = frame.groupby(key, sort=False)
    amt = frame["TransactionAmt"]
    if past_only:
        # Cumulative values in time order: each row sees only the earlier rows of its key.
        n_prev = g.cumcount()
        sum_prev = g["TransactionAmt"].cumsum() - amt
        mean_prev = np.where(n_prev > 0, sum_prev / n_prev.where(n_prev > 0, 1), np.nan)
        frame[f"{prefix}_n"] = n_prev
        frame[f"{prefix}_amt_ratio"] = amt / mean_prev
        frame[f"{prefix}_hours_since"] = g["TransactionDT"].diff() / 3600
        frame[f"{prefix}_n_today"] = frame.groupby([key, "day"], sort=False).cumcount()
    else:
        # Leakage version for dec-02: each row sees all rows of its key, also the later rows.
        frame[f"{prefix}_n"] = g["TransactionAmt"].transform("count")
        frame[f"{prefix}_amt_ratio"] = amt / g["TransactionAmt"].transform("mean")
        frame[f"{prefix}_hours_since"] = g["TransactionDT"].transform(
            lambda s: (s.max() - s.min()) / 3600)
        frame[f"{prefix}_n_today"] = frame.groupby([key, "day"], sort=False)[
            "TransactionAmt"].transform("count")
    return frame


# Earlier transactions of the same key: the customer proxy and the card.
for key, prefix in [("uid", "uid"), ("card1", "card")]:
    txn = add_history(txn, key, prefix)

# Feature lists. Step 4a explains each excluded column (column_status).
HIST = [c for c in txn.columns if c.startswith(("uid_", "card_"))]
EXCLUDE = {"TransactionID", "isFraud", "TransactionDT", "day", "month", "uid", "D1n"}
CAT_COLS = [c for c in txn.columns
            if c not in EXCLUDE and not pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(txn[c])]
NUM_COLS = [c for c in txn.columns
            if c not in EXCLUDE and c not in CAT_COLS and c not in HIST]

N.update({"n_hist": f"{len(HIST)}", "n_num": f"{len(NUM_COLS)}", "n_cat": f"{len(CAT_COLS)}",
          "n_feats": f"{len(NUM_COLS) + len(HIST) + len(CAT_COLS)}",
          "uid_first": f"{(txn['uid_n'] == 0).mean():.0%}"})
fmt(txn[HIST].describe().T[["mean", "50%", "max"]].assign(Empty=txn[HIST].isna().mean()),
    {"mean": "{:,.1f}", "50%": "{:,.1f}", "max": "{:,.0f}", "Empty": "{:.0%}"})

The model gets 100 input columns: 81 numeric columns, 11 text columns and 8 history features. For 34% of the transactions, the uid has no earlier transaction. For these transactions, the amount ratio and the hours since the last transaction are empty: a structural missing value.

2e. Baseline: what does fraud cost if the merchant approves all transactions?

The data is now clean. Before we build a score, we must know the cost that the score must decrease. The simplest policy approves all transactions. It has no false declines and no reviews, so its total cost is the fraud loss.

The fraud loss of a transaction is its amount if it is fraud (as-01: the business pays 100% of the chargeback). The table gives the cost for each 30 days, so that months with a different number of days compare correctly.

Baseline: the fraud loss of approve-all and the fraud rate by month 
# Purpose: Measure the total cost of the approve-all policy by month: the baseline of Step 2e.
# Input:   `txn`, `COST` (as-01).
# Output:  Table `by_month`. Numbers for the text and the business note.

fraud_amt = txn["TransactionAmt"].where(txn["isFraud"] == 1, 0.0)
by_month = txn.assign(fraud_amt=fraud_amt).groupby("month").agg(
    Transactions=("isFraud", "size"), Days=("day", "nunique"), Fraud_rate=("isFraud", "mean"),
    Amount=("TransactionAmt", "sum"), Fraud_amount=("fraud_amt", "sum"))
# Approve-all: each fraud dollar is a loss (as-01). Cost for each 30 days.
by_month["Loss_30"] = by_month["Fraud_amount"] * COST["loss_share"] / by_month["Days"] * 30
by_month["Fraud_share_usd"] = by_month["Fraud_amount"] / by_month["Amount"]
loss_30 = by_month["Loss_30"]
test_loss = (by_month.loc[[5, 6], "Fraud_amount"].sum() * COST["loss_share"]
             / by_month.loc[[5, 6], "Days"].sum() * 30)
N.update({
    "n_txn": f"{len(txn):,}",
    "fraud_rate": f"{txn['isFraud'].mean():.2%}",
    "fraud_amt_share": f"{fraud_amt.sum() / txn['TransactionAmt'].sum():.2%}",
    "txn_per_day": f"{txn.groupby('day').size().mean():,.0f}",
    "base_loss_month": f"${fraud_amt.sum() * COST['loss_share'] / txn['day'].nunique() * 30:,.0f}",
    "base_loss_test": f"${test_loss:,.0f}",
    "base_loss_min": f"${loss_30.min():,.0f}", "base_loss_max": f"${loss_30.max():,.0f}",
    "base_month_max": f"{loss_30.idxmax()}",
    "base_fr_min": f"{by_month['Fraud_rate'].min():.2%}", "base_fr_max": f"{by_month['Fraud_rate'].max():.2%}",
})
del fraud_amt
fmt(by_month.rename(columns={
        "Fraud_rate": "Fraud rate", "Amount": "Amount ($)", "Fraud_amount": "Fraud amount ($)",
        "Loss_30": "Fraud loss, approve-all ($ each 30 days)", "Fraud_share_usd": "Fraud share of $"}),
    {"Transactions": "{:,.0f}", "Fraud rate": "{:.2%}", "Amount ($)": "{:,.0f}",
     "Fraud amount ($)": "{:,.0f}", "Fraud loss, approve-all ($ each 30 days)": "{:,.0f}",

              fontweight="normal", loc="left")
ax1.margins(y=0.15)
# Right: fraud rate by month, with the mean of all months as context.
fr = by_month["Fraud_rate"]
ax2.plot(x, fr, "o-", color=cs.NAVY)
ax2.axhline(txn["isFraud"].mean(), color=cs.GRAY, lw=1, ls="--")
cs.label_end(ax2, x.max(), txn["isFraud"].mean(), "All months", color=cs.GRAY, dy=-8)
for m, v in fr.items():
    ax2.annotate(f"{v:.1%}", (m, v), xytext=(0, 7), textcoords="offset points", ha="center",
                 fontsize=9, color=cs.NAVY)
cs.percent_axis(ax2, decimals=1)
ax2.set_ylim(0, fr.max() * 1.3)
ax2.set_xticks(x)
ax2.set_xticklabels([f"M{m}" for m in x])
ax2.set_title("Fraud rate (share of transactions)", fontsize=9.5, color=cs.MUTED,
              fontweight="normal", loc="left")
mean_loss_k = by_month["Fraud_amount"].sum() * COST["loss_share"] / by_month["Days"].sum() * 30 / 1e3
cs.action_title(fig, f"Approve-all loses about ${mean_loss_k:,.0f}K to fraud every 30 days",
                "Months 1–6, all transactions of the sample, loss = 100% of the fraud amount (as-01)")
plt.show()

How to read: the left panel gives the fraud loss of each month if the merchant approves all transactions, for each 30 days. The right panel gives the share of fraud transactions in each month; the dashed line is the rate of all months.

So what: the fraud loss stays between $450,222 and $643,237 each 30 days, and the fraud rate stays between 2.48% and 4.04%. Fraud is a constant cost, not one bad month. Month 4 has the highest loss. On the test months 5–6, approve-all costs $470,983 each 30 days.

Business note. The data has 590,540 clean transactions, about 3,245 each day, with a fraud rate of 3.50%. Fraud has 3.87% of the dollars. Approve-all costs about $508,326 each 30 days: this is the ceiling of the fraud loss. Two facts limit what a score can promise: the customer key is a proxy, and the label of a customer can follow a later chargeback. Step 3 now splits the data by time, so that the test looks like production.

Step 3. Split data

Step 2 gave clean transactions in time order, a customer key uid and history features from earlier transactions only. It also showed the cost of a policy that approves all transactions. Before we build a score, we must agree on two things. What does “a better policy” mean, and which months give an honest test of it?

Purpose. This step separates the months that train the score from the months that test it, and it fixes the rules of the test. It supports this decision: approve the challenger policy for a test, with a result that is near to the result in production.

Steps 3 to 7 use the same small set of tools: the GBM settings, the metrics, the cost of each action and the policy rules. The code keeps them in the file case02_helpers.py, so that the story stays short. The appendix shows the full file. The next cell loads the tools and gives them the seed and the cost assumptions.

    "b2_level_gap": 0.005,   # Branch 2: |mean score − fraud rate| less than 0.5 points, months 5–6

    "b4_fdr": 0.03,          # Branch 4: decline rate of good transactions 3% or less (as-08)
    "b5_leaf_rate": 0.50,    # Branch 5: leaves with a decline rate of 50% or more ...

3a. What the test must measure

A fraud project has many metrics. A reader can ask: “Why these metrics, and why not others?” Thus we start from the question that each metric answers.

The framework splits the risks of a new policy in two groups. The first group is statistical: the score can fail on the order of the transactions, on the level of the score, or over time. The second group is business: the score can be correct but save no money, or save money but give decisions that fraud operations cannot read. Each failure in production belongs to one branch only. A policy that passes all five branches is ready for a test.

We set the rules in this table before the rerun of this notebook, before we saw the evidence. We do not change a rule after a result. If a result fails a rule, the notebook reports the failure and what it means for the test.

Branch Question Metric Rule
1. Order of risk Does the score put fraud above good transactions better than the champion? PR-AUC, dollar recall in the top 2% (months 5–6) Both above the champion. Model rule: the GBM replaces the logistic regression only if its PR-AUC on month 4 is 10% or more higher (relative).
2. Level Is the mean score equal to the actual fraud rate? Mean score after the recalibration vs. actual fraud rate, months 5–6 A difference of less than 0.5 points
3. Stability Does the score keep its power after the training period? PSI of the score (month 6 vs. months 1–3); PR-AUC on months 5–6 vs. month 4 PSI less than 0.1, and PR-AUC on months 5–6 at 80% or more of month 4
4. Business value Does the policy lower the total cost at the same review capacity? Total cost per month vs. champion; decline rate of good transactions Lower total cost, and a decline rate of good transactions of 3% or less (new assumption as-08: guardrail limit, Marketing to confirm)
5. Explainability Can fraud operations read why the policy declines? Surrogate tree, 3 levels, on the decline decision The leaves with a decline rate of 50% or more hold 50% or more of all declines

The notebook uses each branch in these sections:

  • Branch 1: Step 3b (the split), Step 4b (the model type) and Step 6a.
  • Branch 2: Step 4c (the low fraud rate), Step 5a (the recalibration) and Step 6b.
  • Branch 3: Step 3b and Step 6c. Part 2 adds the PSI of each top feature.
  • Branch 4: Step 5 (the action tiers and the value that puts the transactions in order) and Step 6d.
  • Branch 5: Step 6e.

Branches 1 and 2 are different. A score can put the transactions in the correct order but give a mean score that is too low. The order sets which transactions go to review or decline. The level sets the expected cost in dollars of each action. Thus the notebook checks both.

A fraud decline needs no adverse action notice, as a credit decline does. Branch 5 thus asks for readable rules for fraud operations, not reason codes for each customer.

Technical note. How each metric works:

  • PR-AUC (average precision). Sort the transactions from the highest score. At each fraud transaction in the list, calculate the precision: the share of fraud in all transactions above it. The PR-AUC is the mean of these precisions. A random score gives the fraud rate (0.035 here), and a perfect score gives 1.0. We use the PR-AUC and not only the AUC. With few frauds, the AUC counts many easy good transactions at the bottom of the list. The policy acts only on the top of the list, and the PR-AUC measures the top.
  • Dollar recall in the top 2%. Flag the 2% of transactions with the highest score. Dollar recall = fraud amount in the flagged transactions / all fraud amount. The fraud loss is in dollars, so a score that finds the large frauds is worth more. 2% is near the share of transactions that the policy can decline or review.
  • Calibration (level). Compare the mean score with the actual fraud rate, for all transactions and for each score decile. The expected cost of each action multiplies the score by the amount. Thus a score that is too high declines good customers, and a score that is too low approves fraud.
  • PSI. Cut the score of the reference months into ten bins of equal size. For each bin, compare the share of the reference transactions (e) with the share of the new transactions (a). PSI = Σ (a − e) × ln(a / e). The thresholds 0.1 and 0.25 are the industry convention. The PSI uses no label. Thus it cannot find a change of the fraud patterns when the population stays the same. The PR-AUC rule of branch 3 covers that case.

3b. Which period tests the model?

Which split gives a test result that is near to production?

Why this question matters. The merchant will use the score on the transactions of next month, not on the transactions of last month. If the test uses the wrong transactions, the test result can look good, and the score then fails in production. The policy then promises a decrease of the fraud loss that never comes.

Ways to do it. The split axis is time: where are the test transactions in time, compared with the training transactions? There are four possible answers, and each split method belongs to one of them.

Group Method Advantage Main risk Status
Same period Random split, for example 80/20, k-fold cross-validation, or a split by the customer key uid Simple. Large training set. The two sets have the same fraud rate. Leakage. The same customer is in both sets, and the label after a chargeback (as-07) copies into the test set. The test cannot show a change over time. Possible. Test it.
Earlier period Train on later months, test on earlier months None for this decision. The model uses the future to predict the past. Production never has this data. Screened out
Later period, one cut Out-of-time split: train on months 1–3, validation on month 4, test on months 5–6 Same condition as production: a score from past months gives a score to new transactions. Month 4 sets the policy. Months 5–6 stay clean for the final result. Smaller training set. The test result includes drift, so it is often lower. Possible. Test it.
Later period, many cuts Rolling time windows: train on months 1 to k, test on month k + 1 Shows how fast the score loses power. More fits. Six months give few windows. Possible. Use it as a check. Part 2 retrains on rolling windows (dec-07).

A split by uid removes part of the leakage, but uid is only a proxy for the customer. The data has no customer ID. Thus a split by uid is not a full control.

The out-of-time split needs three sets, not two. The training months fit the score. Month 4 fits all later choices: the recalibration, the thresholds of the policy and the model type. Months 5–6 give only the final result. If the thresholds also used months 5–6, the final result is too good.

Evidence. The code trains the same GBM with the random split and with the out-of-time split. It keeps the GBM of months 1–3 for the next steps. For the check of the decay, it gives the result of that GBM on month 4, month 5 and month 6 separately. These months are one, two and three months after the training period. For each test set, the code measures three branches of the framework:

  • Branch 1, order of risk: the PR-AUC, the AUC, and the recall and the dollar recall in the top 2%.
  • Branch 2, level: the fraud rate of the training set and of the test set.
  • Branch 3, stability: the PSI of the score from the training set to the test set.
Evidence: random split against out-of-time split, with the decay by month 
# Purpose: Compare a random split with an out-of-time split, and show the decay by month (dec-01).
# Input:   `txn` (Step 2), `FEATS`, `CAT_COLS`, `rng`.
# Output:  `train`, `valid`, `test` (the out-of-time split), `m_b` (GBM on months 1–3),
#          `score_valid` (its score on month 4), table `dec01`.

# Out-of-time split: train on months 1–3, set the policy on month 4, test on months 5–6.
train = txn[txn["month"] <= 3]
valid = txn[txn["month"] == 4]
test = txn[txn["month"] >= 5]

# Random split: 20% of all transactions of the six months go to the test set.
is_test_a = rng.random(len(txn)) < 0.2
m_a = fit_gbm(txn[~is_test_a], FEATS, CAT_COLS)
m_b = fit_gbm(train, FEATS, CAT_COLS)
score_valid = predict(m_b, valid)
score_test_b = predict(m_b, test)

# Scores of the training sets, for the PSI (branch 3).
score_train_a = predict(m_a, txn[~is_test_a])
score_train_b = predict(m_b, train)


def split_row(name, tr, te, s_tr, s_te):
    """Return one row of the table: sizes, fraud rates, metrics of branch 1 and the PSI of the score."""
    return {"Split": name, "Training transactions": len(tr), "Test transactions": len(te),
            "Fraud rate, training": tr["isFraud"].mean(), "Fraud rate, test": te["isFraud"].mean(),
            **score_metrics(te, s_te), "PSI of the score": psi(s_tr, s_te)}


is_m5 = (test["month"] == 5).to_numpy()
rows = [
    split_row("A. Random 80/20 (months 1–6 mixed)", txn[~is_test_a], txn[is_test_a],
              score_train_a, predict(m_a, txn[is_test_a])),
    split_row("B. Out-of-time, validation (month 4)", train, valid, score_train_b, score_valid),
    split_row("B. Out-of-time, test (months 5–6)", train, test, score_train_b, score_test_b),
    split_row("Check: month 5 only", train, test[is_m5], score_train_b, score_test_b[is_m5]),
    split_row("Check: month 6 only", train, test[~is_m5], score_train_b, score_test_b[~is_m5]),
]
dec01 = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Split")

rnd, oot_v, oot_t = dec01.iloc[0], dec01.iloc[1], dec01.iloc[2]
N.update({
    "d1_pr_a": f"{rnd['PR-AUC']:.3f}", "d1_pr_b": f"{oot_t['PR-AUC']:.3f}",
    "d1_pr_v": f"{oot_v['PR-AUC']:.3f}",
    "d1_pr_m5": f"{dec01.iloc[3]['PR-AUC']:.3f}", "d1_pr_m6": f"{dec01.iloc[4]['PR-AUC']:.3f}",
    "d1_rec_a": f"{rnd['Recall, top 2%']:.1%}", "d1_rec_b": f"{oot_t['Recall, top 2%']:.1%}",
    "d1_fr_train": f"{train['isFraud'].mean():.2%}", "d1_fr_valid": f"{valid['isFraud'].mean():.2%}",
    "d1_fr_test": f"{test['isFraud'].mean():.2%}",
    "d1_psi_b": f"{oot_t['PSI of the score']:.3f}",
    "d1_keep": f"{oot_t['PR-AUC'] / oot_v['PR-AUC']:.0%}",
    "n_train": f"{len(train):,}", "n_valid": f"{len(valid):,}", "n_test": f"{len(test):,}",
})
fmt(dec01, {"Training transactions": "{:,.0f}", "Test transactions": "{:,.0f}",
            "Fraud rate, training": "{:.2%}", "Fraud rate, test": "{:.2%}", **METRIC_FMT,
            "PSI of the score": "{:.3f}"})

Split
A. Random 80/20 (months 1–6 mixed) 472,258 118,282 3.49% 3.54% 0.790 0.961 54.0% 45.5% 0.000
B. Out-of-time, validation (month 4) 312,574 98,027 3.38% 3.93% 0.574 0.907 39.3% 30.9% 0.014
B. Out-of-time, test (months 5–6) 312,574 179,939 3.38% 3.47% 0.486 0.886 37.3% 26.5% 0.004

How to read: each row is one test set. The rows “Check” use the GBM of months 1–3 on one later month.

So what: the random split gives a much higher PR-AUC than any later month. The PR-AUC goes down with each month after the training period.

Decision. Out-of-time split: train on months 1–3 (312,574 transactions), set the policy on month 4 (98,027), and test on months 5–6 (179,939). The result by month is a check of the speed of decay.

Why. Three reasons, from the most important:

  1. The random split promises too much. It gives a PR-AUC of 0.790. The out-of-time split gives 0.486 on months 5–6. In the top 2% of scores, the random split finds 54.0% of the fraud, and the out-of-time split finds 37.3%. The random split puts later transactions of the same customer in the training set, with the label after a chargeback (as-07). Production never has this information.
  2. Production gives a score to the future. The fraud rate is 3.38% in months 1–3, 3.93% in month 4 and 3.47% in months 5–6. The out-of-time split shows this change of level, so Step 5a can correct it.
  3. It measures the decay of the score. The PR-AUC is 0.574 on month 4, 0.496 on month 5 and 0.478 on month 6. Months 5–6 keep 85% of the PR-AUC of month 4 (branch 3 asks for 80% or more). The PSI of the score is only 0.004. Thus the fraud patterns change faster than the population. Part 2 uses this result to plan the retrain.

What would change the decision. If the data had a true customer ID, a split by customer inside each month can add a second check. It does not replace the out-of-time split.

3c. The champion on the test months

Step 0 defines the champion policy (as-06). It is a decision tree with 3 levels, fit on month 1 with the raw and the time features. The tree does not change after month 1. The fraud rate of each leaf is the score of the champion. Inside a leaf, the larger amount comes first.

The champion uses the same three tiers and the same review capacity as the challenger: 120 alerts each day. Its thresholds come from month 4, with the same method as the challenger. Thus only the score is different. Step 5b gives the formula of the cost of each action.

Parameters of the tree: 3 levels, at least 200 transactions in each leaf, and −999 for a missing value. A tree needs a value in each cell.

Champion: a decision tree with 3 levels on month 1, three tiers, results on months 5–6 
# Purpose: Build the champion (as-06) and give its result on months 5–6: the bar for the challenger.
# Input:   `txn`, `NUM_COLS`, `valid`, `test`, `SEED`.
# Output:  `m1` (month 1), `champ_tree`, `champ_score()`, table `champ_by_month`.

# The champion rules: a decision tree with 3 levels on month 1. A missing value becomes −999.
m1 = txn[txn["month"] == 1]
X_m1 = encode(m1, m1, NUM_COLS, []).fillna(-999)
champ_tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=200, random_state=SEED)
champ_tree.fit(X_m1, m1["isFraud"])


def champ_score(frame):
    """Return the fraud rate of the leaf. Inside a leaf, the larger amount ranks first (as-06)."""
    leaf_rate = champ_tree.predict_proba(encode(frame, m1, NUM_COLS, []).fillna(-999))[:, 1]
    return leaf_rate + 1e-9 * frame["TransactionAmt"].rank(pct=True).to_numpy()


# Three tiers at the same review capacity. The thresholds come from month 4.
champ_rule = fit_policy("prob3", champ_score(valid), valid)
champ_act_test = apply_policy(champ_rule, champ_score(test), test)
rows = [{"Months": "5–6", **summary(test, champ_act_test)}]
for mo in [5, 6]:
    part = (test["month"] == mo).to_numpy()
    rows.append({"Months": str(mo), **summary(test[part], champ_act_test[part])})
champ_by_month = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Months")

c56 = champ_by_month.iloc[0]
N.update({
    "champ_leaves": str(champ_tree.get_n_leaves()),
    "champ_cost": f"${c56['Total cost ($/month)']:,.0f}",
    "champ_stop": f"{c56['Fraud $ stopped']:.1%}",
    "champ_fdr": f"{c56['Decline rate of good transactions']:.2%}",
    "champ_alerts": f"{c56['Alerts each day (mean)']:.0f}",
    "champ_over": f"{c56['Days over capacity']:.0%}",
})
print(export_text(champ_tree, feature_names=list(X_m1.columns), decimals=1))
fmt(champ_by_month, SUM_FMT)

So what: the champion stops only 38.4% of the fraud dollars, and its alerts are more than the capacity on 48% of the days.

The tree has 7 leaves. The size of each leaf changes from day to day, so the alerts of the champion change too. All later comparisons use the same months 5–6 and the same champion.

Business note. We test each policy on months 5–6, as if they are the next two months. On these months, the champion costs $299,432 each month. Step 4. Build models

Step 2 gave each transaction a customer key, a time order and 8 history features. Step 3 fixed the test: train on months 1–3, set the policy on month 4 and measure on months 5–6. This step builds the fraud score that must beat the champion. It first answers which columns the score uses (4a). Then it answers which model gives the score (4b) and how the score handles the low fraud rate (4c).

Purpose. This step builds the fraud score that the policy uses. It supports this decision: the challenger score for the champion/challenger test.

4a. Feature selection

The two files have 434 raw columns. Vesta masked the meaning of most of them. Each column in the model needs a reason that a model risk reviewer accepts. A column that leaks the label makes the test result too good, and the score then fails in production. A column that only repeats another column makes the score slower and harder to monitor.

Why a column leaves the model. The reasons form a funnel with three buckets. The split axes are the time of the information, the stability of the information and the size of the model. Each column gets the first rule that removes it, so the buckets do not overlap. A column that no rule removes is a feature.

Bucket Question Rule Where
1. Not known at the decision Does the business know the value when the transaction arrives? 1. The label (isFraud). History from later transactions is also in this bucket (see the decision below). Step 2b, Step 4a
2. No stable risk information Does the value describe a risk that repeats in a later month? 2. Key or identifier · 3. Time stamp or date Step 2b
3. Removed to keep the model small Does the column add information to the other columns? 4. V column with the same missing pattern as two kept V columns · 5. Masked identity column, not loaded Step 1, Step 4a

Buckets 1 and 2 do not depend on the model. Bucket 3 reduces the size of the data before the model sees it. Its two rules use no label, so they cannot leak the label into the test. The rules of bucket 3 also have a cost: a removed column can carry some extra signal. The funnel accepts this cost, because the GBM must train about 15 times in this notebook.

Rule 4: the V columns. Vesta made 339 V columns from its own data. Many V columns have exactly the same number of empty cells. The columns of one such group often come from the same source of Vesta and carry the same information. The load cell of Step 1 keeps two columns from each group: the two with the most distinct values.

Technical note. For each V column, DuckDB counts the cells that are not empty (COUNT) and the distinct values (approx_count_distinct, a HyperLogLog estimate). The columns with the same count form one group. Inside each group, the code sorts the columns by the number of distinct values and keeps the first two. A column with more distinct values can make more splits in the GBM.

The rule reads no label and no month, so the test months cannot change it. The code saves the counts in a small file, so that later runs do not read the raw CSV again.

Rule 4: groups of V columns with the same count of empty cells 
# Purpose: Count the V groups and the V columns that rule 4 removes (Step 4a funnel).
# Input:   `RAW_TXN`, `V_KEEP`, `DATA_DIR`. The raw CSV only on the first run.
# Output:  `vstat` (one row for each V column: non-empty count, distinct values, group, kept). Table by group size.

VSTAT_FILE = DATA_DIR / "interim" / "fraud_vstat.csv"
if not VSTAT_FILE.exists():
    # One pass over the raw file. The same counts as the load cell of Step 1.
    con = duckdb.connect()
    con.sql(f"""CREATE VIEW t AS SELECT * FROM read_csv('{RAW_TXN.as_posix()}',
                header = true, sample_size = -1)""")
    v_cols = [c for c in con.sql("DESCRIBE t").df()["column_name"] if c.startswith("V")]
    stats = con.sql("SELECT " + ", ".join(
        f"COUNT({c}) AS n_{c}, approx_count_distinct({c}) AS d_{c}" for c in v_cols
    ) + " FROM t").df().iloc[0]
    pd.DataFrame({"col": v_cols, "non_null": [int(stats[f"n_{c}"]) for c in v_cols],
                  "distinct": [int(stats[f"d_{c}"]) for c in v_cols]}).to_csv(VSTAT_FILE, index=False)
    con.close()

vstat = pd.read_csv(VSTAT_FILE)
# Group number: 1 = the group with the most non-empty cells.
order = sorted(vstat["non_null"].unique(), reverse=True)
vstat["group"] = vstat["non_null"].map({v: i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(order)})
vstat["group_size"] = vstat.groupby("group")["col"].transform("size")
vstat["kept"] = vstat["col"].isin(V_KEEP)
vstat["share_empty"] = 1 - vstat["non_null"] / len(txn)
# Check: the kept columns of Step 1 must be at most two in each group.
assert vstat.groupby("group")["kept"].sum().le(2).all(), "Rule 4 keeps at most two columns in each group."

v_by_size = (vstat.groupby("group").agg(size=("col", "size"), kept=("kept", "sum"))
             .groupby("size").agg(Groups=("kept", "size"), Kept=("kept", "sum")))
v_by_size["V columns"] = v_by_size.index * v_by_size["Groups"]
v_by_size["Removed"] = v_by_size["V columns"] - v_by_size["Kept"]
v_by_size.index.name = "Columns in the group"
N.update({"n_v": f"{len(vstat)}", "n_vgroups": f"{vstat['group'].nunique()}",
          "n_vkept": f"{int(vstat['kept'].sum())}", "n_vremoved": f"{int((~vstat['kept']).sum())}",
          "v_big": f"{int(vstat['group_size'].max())}",
          "v_small": f"{int(vstat['group_size'].min())}"})

The 339 V columns form 15 groups. The groups have from 11 to 46 columns. In total, rule 4 keeps 30 V columns and removes 309.

Rule 5: the identity columns. Only about one quarter of the transactions have a row in the identity file. Step 1 loads the five identity columns that people can read. They give the device type, the device name, the system (id_30), the browser (id_31) and the screen size (id_33). The other id_ columns hold masked codes of the network and the device. The flag has_identity keeps the main signal of the identity file for all transactions.

History features. The last group of columns comes from Step 2d: the history features of each customer. They are the only columns that read other transactions, so they are the main risk of leakage. The decision below examines them.

Which customer history can the model use?

Why this question matters. A fraud often looks normal alone, but not against the earlier behavior of the card. For example, a fraud can have an amount ten times the usual amount, or many transactions in one hour. But the label after a chargeback (as-07) puts many fraud labels on the later transactions of the same customer. A history feature that reads these later transactions copies the label. The test then promises a fraud loss decrease that production does not give.

Ways to do it. The split axis is the set of transactions of the same key that a feature reads at the time of the decision:

Group Advantage Main risk Screen
A. No transactions of the key: no history No risk of leakage. Simple. The score does not see a change from the normal behavior of the customer. Test
B. Earlier transactions only The business has the same information at the time of the decision. It shows a change of behavior. More code. A new customer has no history. The counts grow over time (Part 2). Test
C. All transactions, also the later ones The highest test result. Many Kaggle solutions use it. Leakage. It reads the future and the label after a chargeback (as-07). Test, to measure the leakage
B2. Earlier transactions plus their labels (“earlier fraud of this customer”) A strong signal: Step 2b shows the high fraud rate after an earlier fraud. The business learns a label only from the chargeback, weeks later. Screened out: the data has no chargeback dates, so the code cannot know when a label became known.

A history window of fixed length (for example 90 days) is a variant of group B. It changes the drift of the features, not the leakage, so Part 2 discusses it.

Evidence. The code trains the same GBM on months 1–3 with groups A, B and C, and scores month 4. It uses the metrics of branch 1 (Step 3a): PR-AUC and the dollar recall in the top 2% of the scores. For group C, the code makes the history features again over all transactions of each key (add_history(..., past_only=False)).

Evidence: three sets of history features, metrics on month 4 
# Purpose: Compare no history, history from earlier transactions and history from all transactions (dec-02).
# Input:   `txn`, `train`, `valid`, `HIST`, `NUM_COLS`, `CAT_COLS`, `FEATS`, `score_valid`, `fit_gbm()`.
# Output:  Table `dec02` (metrics on month 4 for each group).

# Group C: the leakage version of the history features.
leak = txn[["uid", "card1", "day", "TransactionAmt", "TransactionDT"]].copy()
for key, prefix in [("uid", "uid"), ("card1", "card")]:
    leak = add_history(leak, key, prefix, past_only=False)
txn_leak = txn.drop(columns=HIST).join(leak[HIST])
del leak

m_02a = fit_gbm(train, NUM_COLS, CAT_COLS)                       # A. No history
m_02c = fit_gbm(txn_leak[txn_leak["month"] <= 3], FEATS, CAT_COLS)  # C. All transactions
# B is the GBM of Step 3 (`score_valid`): the same features as the challenger.
dec02 = pd.DataFrame([
    {"Option": "A. No history", **score_metrics(valid, predict(m_02a, valid))},
    {"Option": "B. Earlier transactions only", **score_metrics(valid, score_valid)},
    {"Option": "C. All transactions (leakage)",
     **score_metrics(valid, predict(m_02c, txn_leak[txn_leak["month"] == 4]))},
]).set_index("Option")
del txn_leak, m_02c
N.update({f"d2_pr_{k}": f"{v:.3f}" for k, v in zip("abc", dec02["PR-AUC"])})
N.update({f"d2_usd_{k}": f"{v:.1%}" for k, v in zip("abc", dec02["Dollar recall, top 2%"])})
N.update({"d2_gain_b": f"{dec02['PR-AUC'].iloc[1] / dec02['PR-AUC'].iloc[0] - 1:+.0%}",
          "d2_gain_c": f"{dec02['PR-AUC'].iloc[2] / dec02['PR-AUC'].iloc[1] - 1:+.0%}"})
fmt(dec02, METRIC_FMT)
PR-AUC AUC Recall, top 2% Dollar recall, top 2%
Option
A. No history 0.570 0.903 39.3% 32.3%
B. Earlier transactions only 0.574 0.907 39.3% 30.9%
C. All transactions (leakage) 0.599 0.916 41.4% 32.0%

Decision. Use history features from earlier transactions only (group B). Do not use history from later transactions or earlier labels.

Why. On month 4, the PR-AUC is 0.570 with no history, 0.574 with earlier transactions and 0.599 with all transactions. In the top 2% of the scores, the three groups find 32.3%, 30.9% and 32.0% of the fraud dollars.

The earlier history changes the PR-AUC by +1% against no history, and it does not increase the dollar recall. Thus the history adds little power to the score on month 4. We keep it for two other uses. They are readable, so the rules of the surrogate tree (Step 6) use them. They are also the base for a feature “earlier fraud of this customer” when the chargeback dates exist.

Group C gives a further +4% on the PR-AUC. Production cannot give these features, so this gain is leakage. The gain is small on month 4, because the model trains only on months 1–3. A random split puts the same customers in the training data and in the test, and the leakage then grows (Step 3).

What would change the decision. If the surrogate tree and the fraud analysts do not use the history features, then group A is simpler and as strong. Then remove the history features.

Status of each column: bucket, rule and detail (one row for each column) 
# Purpose: Give each raw column of the two files and each engineered feature its bucket, rule and detail.
# Input:   `RAW_TXN`, `RAW_ID`, `txn`, `vstat`, `V_KEEP`, `NUM_COLS`, `CAT_COLS`, `HIST`.
# Output:  `column_status` (columns: column, group, bucket, rule, detail; contract C4), funnel table.

RULE_BUCKET = {
    "1. Label": "1. Not known at the decision",
    "2. Key or identifier": "2. No stable risk information",
    "3. Time stamp or date": "2. No stable risk information",
    "4. V column with the same missing pattern": "3. Removed to keep the model small",
    "5. Masked identity column, not loaded": "3. Removed to keep the model small",
    "Feature": "Feature",
}
# Raw column names: the header rows of the two files only.
if RAW_TXN.exists() and RAW_ID.exists():
    raw_txn_cols = list(pd.read_csv(RAW_TXN, nrows=0).columns)
    raw_id_cols = [c for c in pd.read_csv(RAW_ID, nrows=0).columns if c != "TransactionID"]
else:  # Only the Parquet file exists: the names follow the Vesta pattern.
    raw_txn_cols = (["TransactionID", "isFraud", "TransactionDT", "TransactionAmt", "ProductCD"]
                    + [f"card{i}" for i in range(1, 7)] + ["addr1", "addr2", "dist1", "dist2"]
                    + ["P_emaildomain", "R_emaildomain"] + [f"C{i}" for i in range(1, 15)]
                    + [f"D{i}" for i in range(1, 16)] + [f"M{i}" for i in range(1, 10)]
                    + [f"V{i}" for i in range(1, 340)])
    raw_id_cols = [f"id_{i:02d}" for i in range(1, 39)] + ["DeviceType", "DeviceInfo"]
ENGINEERED = ["day", "month", "hour", "D1n", "uid", "log_amt", "cents", "email_match", "has_identity"] + HIST
FEATURE_SET = set(NUM_COLS) | set(CAT_COLS) | set(HIST)


def col_group(c):
    """Column group of one column (the groups of Step 1b and Step 2d)."""
    if c in ("TransactionID", "isFraud"):
        return "Key and label"
    if c in ("TransactionDT", "day", "month", "hour"):
        return "Time"
    if c in HIST:
        return "Engineered: history"
    if c in ("D1n", "uid"):
        return "Engineered: customer key"
    if c in ("log_amt", "cents", "email_match", "has_identity"):
        return "Engineered: same transaction"
    for prefix, name in [("card", "Card"), ("addr", "Address"), ("dist", "Distance"), ("C", "C: counts"),
                         ("D", "D: time deltas"), ("M", "M: match flags"), ("V", "V: Vesta features"),
                         ("id_", "Identity: id_"), ("Device", "Identity: device")]:
        if c.startswith(prefix) and (prefix not in ("C", "D", "M", "V") or c[1:].isdigit()):
            return name
    if c.endswith("emaildomain"):
        return "Email domain"
    return {"TransactionAmt": "Amount", "ProductCD": "Product"}.get(c, "Other")


def col_rule(c):
    """The first rule of the funnel that removes the column, or Feature."""
    if c == "isFraud":
        return "1. Label"
    if c in ("TransactionID", "uid"):
        return "2. Key or identifier"
    if c in ("TransactionDT", "day", "month", "D1n"):
        return "3. Time stamp or date"
    if c in FEATURE_SET:
        return "Feature"
    if c.startswith("V"):
        return "4. V column with the same missing pattern"
    if c in raw_id_cols:
        return "5. Masked identity column, not loaded"
    raise ValueError(f"No rule for column {c}")


# Empty share of the identity columns that Step 1 does not load: from the identity file (144,000 rows).
id_not_loaded = [c for c in raw_id_cols if c not in txn.columns]
id_nonempty = (pd.read_csv(RAW_ID, usecols=id_not_loaded).notna().sum()
               if RAW_ID.exists() else pd.Series(dtype=float))
v_info = vstat.set_index("col")
v_kept_in = vstat[vstat["kept"]].groupby("group")["col"].agg(", ".join)
DETAIL = {
    "isFraud": "Target. Includes later transactions after a chargeback (as-07)",
    "TransactionID": "Key of both files",
    "uid": "Customer proxy (card1 + addr1 + D1n); key of the history features",
    "TransactionDT": "Time order of the rows and the split (Step 3)",
    "day": "Day number; history and capacity by day", "month": "Split and results by month (Step 3)",
    "D1n": "First day of the card; a date that moves each month (Step 2b, Part 2)",
}


def col_detail(c, rule):
    """Short text with the evidence for the status of one column."""
    if c in DETAIL:
        return DETAIL[c]
    if c in v_info.index:
        r = v_info.loc[c]
        text = (f"Group {r['group']} ({r['group_size']} columns, {r['share_empty']:.0%} empty); "
                f"{r['distinct']:,} distinct values")
        return text if r["kept"] else text + f"; group keeps {v_kept_in.get(r['group'], 'none')}"
    if rule.startswith("5."):
        return (f"Not empty for {id_nonempty[c] / len(txn):.1%} of the transactions"
                if c in id_nonempty.index else "Masked code")
    kind = "text" if c in CAT_COLS else "history" if c in HIST else "numeric"
    return f"{kind}; {txn[c].isna().mean():.0%} empty"


cols = list(dict.fromkeys(raw_txn_cols + raw_id_cols + ENGINEERED))
column_status = pd.DataFrame({"column": cols})
column_status["group"] = column_status["column"].map(col_group)
column_status["rule"] = column_status["column"].map(col_rule)
column_status["bucket"] = column_status["rule"].map(RULE_BUCKET)
column_status["detail"] = [col_detail(c, r) for c, r in zip(column_status["column"], column_status["rule"])]
column_status = column_status[["column", "group", "bucket", "rule", "detail"]]
# Checks: each model input has the status Feature, and each feature is an input of the model.
assert set(column_status.loc[column_status["rule"] == "Feature", "column"]) == FEATURE_SET
assert column_status["column"].is_unique

feat = column_status[column_status["rule"] == "Feature"]
N.update({"n_features": f"{len(feat)}",
          "n_feat_raw": f"{int((~feat['column'].isin(ENGINEERED)).sum())}",
          "n_feat_eng": f"{int(feat['column'].isin(ENGINEERED).sum())}",
          "n_id_out": f"{len(id_not_loaded)}"})
# Funnel table: the columns that each rule removes, by bucket.
funnel = (column_status.groupby(["bucket", "rule"])["column"]
          .agg(Columns="size", Examples=lambda c: ", ".join(list(c)[:5])).reset_index()
          .rename(columns={"bucket": "Bucket", "rule": "Rule"}).set_index(["Bucket", "Rule"]))
funnel
