The funnel reads 434 raw columns of the two files and the engineered columns of Step 2. It keeps 100 features: 87 raw columns and 13 engineered features. Rule 5 removes 35 masked identity columns. Appendix A gives the status of each column group and of each column that the model uses.

4b. Model type

Section 4a fixed the columns of the score, with history features from earlier transactions only. The champion uses the same raw columns in a tree with 3 levels. The next question is: which type of model gives the score, and is the extra power worth the cost?

Which model gives the fraud score?

Why this question matters. The model type sets how much fraud the score finds in the top of the list, where the policy acts. It also sets how fast the score runs in the payment flow and how easily fraud operations can read the decisions. A model that finds more fraud but cannot score a payment in milliseconds cannot go into production.

Ways to do it. The first split axis is the label: does the model learn from the fraud label? The models that learn from the label then split by how they make a decision. These five groups cover the common models, and each model belongs to one group. Each group then goes through three filters:

  • Predictive power on this table. The data has 312,574 training transactions, text features with many levels, and many missing values.
  • Readable for fraud operations. A fraud decline needs no adverse action notice. But fraud operations must find new fraud patterns and answer a partner who asks “why this decline?” (branch 5).
  • Deployment and control. The model must give a score in real time, the same score each day, and the team must retrain it each month (Part 2).
Group: how the model decides Models Predictive power Readable Deployment Result
No label: a transaction is fraud if it is far from normal transactions Isolation forest, autoencoder Low. Many frauds look like normal purchases. The data has the label, so a method without it throws away information. Poor. “Far from normal” is not a reason. Simple. Screened out
Distance or geometry: a transaction is fraud if it is near past frauds or on the wrong side of a boundary KNN, SVM Medium. They need scaled numbers and no missing values. Poor. KNN keeps all training transactions in the system. It is too slow for real time. Screened out
Connectionist: many layers of weights learn new features Neural networks Strong on sequences of transactions. On this table, usually not better than tree ensembles. Poor. A black box. More effort to fit, to monitor and to retrain each month. Screened out
Trees and rules: the model splits the transactions by rules Decision tree, random forest, GBM GBM: usually the best on tables with missing values. One tree: weak, but it is the champion (as-06). Random forest: strong, but usually below the GBM. One tree: strong. GBM: medium. Step 6e adds readable rules with a surrogate tree. Standard in fraud systems. Fast. Keep the GBM. Keep the tree as the champion.
Parametric: one equation with one weight for each feature Naive Bayes, logistic regression Naive Bayes assumes that the features are independent. That is not true here (the count features move together). Logistic regression: good on a straight line in each feature. Strong in principle. But Vesta masked most features, so a weight has little meaning. Simple and fast. Keep the logistic regression

The shortlist has three models: the champion tree, the logistic regression and the GBM. The logistic regression is the simple challenger: easy to deploy, but it adds the effect of each feature without interactions. The GBM finds interactions, for example “a new card and a large amount at night”. It also uses a missing value as information.

The rule before the evidence (branch 1). The challenger score is the logistic regression, unless the GBM has a PR-AUC on month 4 that is 10% or more higher (relative). We set this rule in section 3a, before the rerun. A more complex model must earn its place with a clear gain.

Technical note. Settings of the two challenger models. Both use the training months 1–3 and the same features: the raw and the time features plus the history features.

  • Logistic regression. For each number: fill a missing value with the median and add a flag for “missing”. Then change the number to a normal distribution with a quantile transform (100 quantiles). For each text feature: one column for each level with 200 or more transactions. Regularization C = 0.1.
  • GBM. The settings are in GBM_PARAMS (case02_helpers.py). The learning rate is 0.08, with at most 400 trees. Each tree has at most 63 leaves, and each leaf has at least 100 transactions. The L2 regularization is 1.0. An early stop uses 10% of the training rows. A text feature with 200 levels or fewer becomes a category. A text feature with more levels becomes its frequency in the training data. The GBM has no imputation: it learns the best side of each split for a missing value.
  • Champion. The tree of Step 3c (as-06), on month 1 only.

Evidence. The code trains the logistic regression and compares the three models on month 4, the validation month. The months 5–6 stay clean for Step 6. The table gives branch 1: the PR-AUC, the AUC, and the recall and the dollar recall in the top 2%.

Evidence: champion rules, logistic regression and GBM on month 4 
# Purpose: Compare the champion, the logistic regression and the GBM on month 4, and apply the
#          model rule of branch 1 (dec-03).
# Input:   `train`, `valid`, `champ_score()`, `score_valid` (GBM, Step 3b), `NUM_COLS`, `HIST`, `CAT_COLS`.
# Output:  `lr`, `lr_cols`, `score_valid_lr`, table `dec03`, `d3_gain` (relative PR-AUC gain of the GBM).

# Logistic regression: quantile transform for numbers, one column for each frequent level of a text feature.
num_lr = NUM_COLS + HIST
lr = make_pipeline(
    ColumnTransformer([
        ("num", make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median", add_indicator=True),
                              QuantileTransformer(n_quantiles=100, output_distribution="normal",
                                                  subsample=100_000, random_state=SEED)), num_lr),
        ("cat", make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value="missing"),
                              OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist",
                                            min_frequency=200)), CAT_COLS),
    ]),
    LogisticRegression(C=0.1, max_iter=1000),
)
lr_cols = num_lr + CAT_COLS
lr.fit(train[lr_cols].astype({c: object for c in CAT_COLS}), train["isFraud"])
score_valid_lr = lr.predict_proba(valid[lr_cols].astype({c: object for c in CAT_COLS}))[:, 1]
score_valid_champ = champ_score(valid)

dec03 = pd.DataFrame([
    {"Model": "Champion: decision tree, 3 levels (month 1)", **score_metrics(valid, score_valid_champ)},
    {"Model": "Logistic regression", **score_metrics(valid, score_valid_lr)},
    {"Model": "GBM", **score_metrics(valid, score_valid)},
]).set_index("Model")

# The model rule of branch 1, set before the evidence: the GBM needs a 10% higher PR-AUC (relative).
d3_gain = dec03.iloc[2]["PR-AUC"] / dec03.iloc[1]["PR-AUC"] - 1
d3_pass = d3_gain >= RULES["b1_model_gain"]
N.update({f"d3_pr_{k}": f"{v:.3f}" for k, v in zip("abc", dec03["PR-AUC"])})
N.update({f"d3_usd_{k}": f"{v:.1%}" for k, v in zip("abc", dec03["Dollar recall, top 2%"])})
N.update({"d3_gain": f"{d3_gain:.0%}", "d3_rule": "passes" if d3_pass else "fails",
          "d3_vs_rule": "more than" if d3_pass else "less than",
          "d4_one_in": f"{round(1 / train['isFraud'].mean())}"})
fmt(dec03, METRIC_FMT)

How to read: each line starts at the transaction with the highest score and adds transactions in the order of the score. The height is the share of all fraud dollars of month 4 that the flagged transactions hold.

So what: at the top 2%, the GBM finds 30.9% of the fraud dollars, against 17.2% for the champion. Thus the GBM finds more fraud dollars for the same review and decline work.

Decision. The challenger score is the GBM. The GBM passes the model rule of branch 1 that we set before the evidence. The logistic regression stays as a check.

Why. On month 4, the PR-AUC is 0.268 for the champion, 0.329 for the logistic regression and 0.574 for the GBM. Thus the GBM is 75% higher than the logistic regression, more than the limit of 10% in the rule.

The business result agrees. In the top 2% of scores, the GBM finds 30.9% of the fraud dollars. The champion finds 17.2% and the logistic regression finds 16.1%.

The GBM is harder to read than a tree or a weight table. That cost is smaller here than in a credit decision:

  • A fraud decline needs no adverse action notice. Fraud operations need readable patterns, not a reason for each customer.
  • Vesta masked most features, so the weights of the logistic regression are not readable either.
  • Step 6e gives readable rules with a surrogate tree on the decline decision (branch 5).

What would change the decision. A regulator or a partner can require a reason for each decline. Then use the logistic regression for the decline tier and the GBM for the review tier.

4c. Low fraud rate: class imbalance and the level of the score

The GBM puts the fraud transactions at the top of the list better than the other models. But Step 5 multiplies the score by the amount to get the expected cost in dollars. Thus the level of the score must also be correct (branch 2). Two different problems can make the level wrong, and teams often mix them.

  1. Class imbalance. Only about one transaction in 30 is fraud. Some teams then give more weight to fraud, with a class weight, with fewer good transactions in the training data, or with synthetic fraud (SMOTE). These methods make the model behave as if fraud is more common than it is. Thus they push the score up, far above the real fraud rate.
  2. A change of level over time. The fraud rate is 3.38% in months 1–3 and 3.93% in month 4 (Step 3b). A model that learns from months 1–3 gives a score at the level of months 1–3.

The second problem is the more dangerous one, because it hides in the money. The chain is:

A level that is too low → expected fraud loss too low → too many approvals of fraud. A level that is too high → expected cost of an approval too high → too many declines of good customers.

How do we handle the low fraud rate?

Why this question matters. The score enters the expected cost of each action in dollars (Step 5b). A score that is too high declines good customers. A score that is too low approves fraud.

Ways to do it. The split axis is where the correction happens: in the training data, in the model, or after the model. These three places cover all methods.

Where Method Advantage Main risk Status
Training data A random sample of the good transactions: 4 good transactions for each fraud Faster training. Balanced classes. It removes data. The score becomes too high. Test it
Training data SMOTE: synthetic fraud from the fraud transactions Balanced classes. Synthetic rows from text features and missing values have no clear meaning. The score becomes too high. Screened out: the same effect as the sample, with more risk
Model Class weight “balanced”: each fraud counts more in the fit More weight to fraud. The score becomes too high. It needs a recalibration after the fit. Test it
After the model No change in the fit. Then move the level of the score to the fraud rate of the most recent month (recalibration). The score stays near the real rate. One constant to explain. It needs a recent month with known labels. Test it

Evidence. The code trains the same GBM again on months 1–3, one time with the class weight and one time on the sample. It gives the PR-AUC (branch 1), the mean score and the actual fraud rate on month 4 (branch 2). The chart then compares the mean score with the actual fraud rate for each score decile.

Evidence: class weight and a sample of the good transactions against no change 
# Purpose: Compare three ways to handle the low fraud rate on month 4 (dec-04).
# Input:   `train`, `valid`, `score_valid` (no change), `FEATS`, `CAT_COLS`, `rng`.
# Output:  `m_04b`, `m_04c`, `score_valid_w` (class weight), table `dec04`.

# The sample: all fraud of months 1–3 and 4 random good transactions for each fraud.
fraud_idx = train.index[train["isFraud"] == 1]
good_idx = train.index[train["isFraud"] == 0]
under = train.loc[np.r_[fraud_idx, rng.choice(good_idx, 4 * len(fraud_idx), replace=False)]]
m_04b = fit_gbm(train, FEATS, CAT_COLS, class_weight="balanced")
m_04c = fit_gbm(train, FEATS, CAT_COLS, sample=under)
score_valid_w = predict(m_04b, valid)

rows = []
for name, s in [("A. No change", score_valid), ("B. Class weight", score_valid_w),
                ("C. Sample, 1 fraud for 4 good", predict(m_04c, valid))]:
    rows.append({"Option": name, "PR-AUC": average_precision_score(valid["isFraud"], s),
                 "Mean score": s.mean(), "Actual fraud rate": valid["isFraud"].mean()})
dec04 = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Option")
N.update({"d4_mean_a": f"{dec04.iloc[0]['Mean score']:.2%}",
          "d4_mean_b": f"{dec04.iloc[1]['Mean score']:.1%}",
          "d4_mean_c": f"{dec04.iloc[2]['Mean score']:.1%}",
          "d4_actual": f"{valid['isFraud'].mean():.2%}",
          "d4_pr": " / ".join(f"{v:.3f}" for v in dec04["PR-AUC"])})
fmt(dec04, {"PR-AUC": "{:.3f}", "Mean score": "{:.2%}", "Actual fraud rate": "{:.2%}"})
PR-AUC Mean score Actual fraud rate
Option
A. No change 0.574 2.68% 3.93%
B. Class weight 0.542 11.82% 3.93%
C. Sample, 1 fraud for 4 good 0.557 8.13% 3.93%
Chart: mean score against the actual fraud rate by score decile, month 4 
# Purpose: Show the calibration by score decile, with no change and with the class weight (dec-04).
# Input:   `valid`, `score_valid`, `score_valid_w`.
# Output:  Calibration chart, table `calib04`.

# Deciles of the score with no change. Decile 10 holds the 10% of transactions with the highest score.
calib04 = pd.DataFrame({
    "decile": pd.qcut(pd.Series(score_valid).rank(method="first"), 10, labels=False) + 1,
    "Actual": valid["isFraud"].to_numpy(),
    "No change": score_valid,
    "Class weight": score_valid_w,
}).groupby("decile").mean()
top = calib04.loc[10]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
styles = {"Actual": (cs.GRAY, "o", "Actual fraud rate"), "No change": (cs.NAVY, "s", "GBM, no change"),
          "Class weight": (cs.BLUE, "^", "GBM, class weight")}
for col, (color, marker, label) in styles.items():
    ax.plot(calib04.index, calib04[col], marker=marker, color=color, lw=1.5 if col == "Actual" else 2)
    # "Actual" and "No change" end near the same point. A vertical offset keeps the labels apart.
    dy = {"Actual": 7, "No change": -7, "Class weight": 0}[col]
    cs.label_end(ax, calib04.index[-1], calib04[col].iloc[-1], label, color=color, dy=dy,
                 bold=(col == "Class weight"))
ax.set_xlabel("Score decile of the GBM with no change (10 = highest score)")
ax.set_ylabel("Fraud rate or mean score")
ax.set_xticks(calib04.index)
ax.set_xlim(0.5, 12.9)
cs.percent_axis(ax)
cs.action_title(fig, f"A class weight puts the mean score at {score_valid_w.mean():.0%} against "
                     f"{valid['isFraud'].mean():.1%} actual fraud",
                "Mean score and actual fraud rate by score decile, month 4 (validation)")
plt.show()

N.update({"d4_top_actual": f"{top['Actual']:.1%}", "d4_top_none": f"{top['No change']:.1%}",
          "d4_top_w": f"{top['Class weight']:.1%}"})

How to read: each point is one tenth of the transactions of month 4, in the order of the GBM score. The gray line is the actual fraud rate. The navy line is the GBM with no change. The blue line is the GBM with the class weight.

So what: the class weight puts the score above the actual fraud rate in each decile. With no change, the score is below the actual fraud rate in each decile.

Decision. No class weight, no sample and no SMOTE. In Step 5a, move the level of the score to the fraud rate of month 4 (recalibration).

Why. The PR-AUC of options A, B and C is 0.574 / 0.542 / 0.557. Thus the order of the transactions changes little (branch 1). But the mean score is 11.8% with the class weight and 8.1% with the sample. The actual fraud rate is 3.93% (branch 2 fails for both).

In the top decile, the class weight gives a mean score of 54.6% against an actual fraud rate of 28.0%. The policy in Step 5 then declines too many good customers.

With no change, the mean score is 2.68%, below the actual fraud rate in each decile. The order is correct, but the level is too low. One constant on the log-odds scale corrects the level and keeps the order. Step 5a applies it.

What would change the decision. If the policy uses only the order of the transactions, for example a fixed number of alerts each day, the level has no effect. Then a class weight or a sample can be useful if it increases the PR-AUC.

Business note. The challenger score is a GBM on the raw, time and history features. On month 4, its PR-AUC is 0.574, against 0.268 for the champion rules. In the top 2%, it finds 30.9% of the fraud dollars. Its level is too low for month 4, and the policy needs a correct level. Step 5 corrects the level and changes the score into an action for each transaction.

Step 5. Make predictions and actions

Step 4 selected the GBM as the challenger score. It left two open points. The level of the score is too low for month 4, and a score alone does not stop fraud. This step closes both points: what score does each transaction get, and what action does the policy take on it?

Purpose. This step gives each transaction a fraud score at the correct level and one action: approve, review or decline. It supports this decision: the challenger policy for the champion/challenger test.

5a. Recalibration of the score

Section 4c found that the mean score of the GBM is 2.68% on month 4, but the actual fraud rate is 3.93%. If we do not correct this, the expected fraud loss of an approval is too low. The policy then approves fraud that a review or a decline can stop.

The correction uses one constant on the log-odds scale. The code adds the constant to the log-odds of each score. The constant makes the mean score of month 4 equal to the fraud rate of month 4. Months 5–6 then check the result. The recalibration does not change the order of the transactions. Thus the PR-AUC and the dollar recall do not change.

Technical note. Score after the recalibration = 1 / (1 + exp(−(ln(p / (1 − p)) + δ))), with the function shift_logodds(). The code finds the constant δ (DELTA) with a root search (Brent’s method) between −5 and 5. On the log-odds scale, one constant keeps the order of the transactions and keeps each score between 0 and 1.

In production, the team uses the most recent month with known labels. Here month 4 has this role. Months 5–6 are an honest check, because the constant never sees them.

Recalibration: one shift of the log-odds, fit on month 4, checked on months 5–6 
# Purpose: Move the score to the fraud rate of month 4 with one constant on the log-odds scale (dec-04).
# Input:   `score_valid` (GBM on month 4), `m_b`, `valid`, `test`, `shift_logodds()` (case02_helpers.py).
# Output:  `DELTA` (the constant), `p_valid` (score of month 4), `p_test` (score of months 5–6), table `recal`.

# Find the constant that makes the mean score of month 4 equal to its fraud rate.
DELTA = brentq(lambda d: shift_logodds(score_valid, d).mean() - valid["isFraud"].mean(), -5, 5)
p_valid = shift_logodds(score_valid, DELTA)
score_test = predict(m_b, test)  # Score of months 5–6 before the recalibration
p_test = shift_logodds(score_test, DELTA)

recal = pd.DataFrame({
    "Sample": ["Month 4 (calibration)", "Months 5–6 (check)"],
    "Actual fraud rate": [valid["isFraud"].mean(), test["isFraud"].mean()],
    "Mean score before": [score_valid.mean(), score_test.mean()],
    "Mean score after": [p_valid.mean(), p_test.mean()],
}).set_index("Sample")
gap_test = p_test.mean() - test["isFraud"].mean()
N.update({"delta": f"{DELTA:+.2f}", "calib_before": f"{score_test.mean():.2%}",
          "calib_test": f"{p_test.mean():.2%}", "fraud_test": f"{test['isFraud'].mean():.2%}",
          "calib_gap": f"{abs(gap_test) * 100:.2f}",
          "calib_vs_rule": "less than" if abs(gap_test) < RULES["b2_level_gap"] else "more than"})
fmt(recal, {c: "{:.2%}" for c in recal.columns})
Actual fraud rate Mean score before Mean score after
Sample
Month 4 (calibration) 3.93% 2.68% 3.93%
Months 5–6 (check) 3.47% 2.31% 3.41%

The constant is +0.69 on the log-odds scale. On months 5–6, the mean score goes from 2.31% before the recalibration to 3.41% after it. The actual fraud rate is 3.47%. The difference is 0.06 points, less than the limit of 0.5 points of branch 2. Step 6b gives the full check by score decile.

5b. Cost of each action

The score tells how likely a fraud is. The business decision is about money. Thus each action gets an expected cost in dollars, from the score and the amount. Each action has a different type of cost:

  • Approve. If the transaction is fraud, the merchant pays the chargeback (as-01).
  • Decline. If the transaction is good, the merchant loses the margin and the customer has friction (as-02).
  • Review. An analyst examines the transaction before the approval. The analyst stops most of the fraud, and a good customer waits a short time (as-05).

The analysts have a fixed cost for each day (as-04). Thus a review has no extra analyst cost inside the review capacity. The next cell lists the cost assumptions and gives an example for two amounts with the same score.

Cost assumptions and an example: two amounts with the same fraud score 
# Purpose: Show the cost assumptions (as-01 to as-05) and the expected cost of each action for an example.
# Input:   `COST`, `expected_costs()`, `capacity()` (case02_helpers.py).
# Output:  Table `cost_example`. N values for the text of Step 5b.

EX_P = 0.10  # The fraud score of the example
EX_AMT = [50.0, 1000.0]  # A small and a large amount
cost_example = pd.DataFrame([
    dict(zip(["Amount ($)", "Approve ($)", "Decline ($)", "Review ($)"],
             [amt, *[float(v) for v in expected_costs(EX_P, amt)]]))
    for amt in EX_AMT
]).set_index("Amount ($)")
cost_example["Cheapest without review"] = np.where(
    cost_example["Approve ($)"] <= cost_example["Decline ($)"], "Approve", "Decline")
cost_example["Decrease from a review ($)"] = (
    cost_example[["Approve ($)", "Decline ($)"]].min(axis=1) - cost_example["Review ($)"])

N.update({
    "loss_share": f"{COST['loss_share']:.0%}", "fd_margin": f"{COST['fd_margin']:.0%}",
    "fd_friction": f"${COST['fd_friction']:.0f}", "review_catch": f"{COST['review_catch']:.0%}",
    "review_friction": f"${COST['review_friction']:.0f}", "analysts": str(COST["analysts"]),
    "alerts_per_analyst": str(COST["alerts_per_analyst"]),
    "ex_p": f"{EX_P:.0%}", "ex_s": f"${EX_AMT[0]:,.0f}", "ex_l": f"${EX_AMT[1]:,.0f}",
    "ex_gain_50": f"${cost_example.iloc[0]['Decrease from a review ($)']:,.2f}",
    "ex_gain_1000": f"${cost_example.iloc[1]['Decrease from a review ($)']:,.2f}",
    "ex_act_50": cost_example.iloc[0]["Cheapest without review"].lower(),
    "ex_act_1000": cost_example.iloc[1]["Cheapest without review"].lower(),
})
fmt(cost_example.reset_index(), {"Amount ($)": "{:,.0f}", "Approve ($)": "{:,.2f}", "Decline ($)": "{:,.2f}",
                                 "Review ($)": "{:,.2f}", "Decrease from a review ($)": "{:,.2f}"})
Amount ($) Approve ($) Decline ($) Review ($) Cheapest without review Decrease from a review ($)
0 50 5.00 10.35 2.30 Approve 2.70
1 1,000 100.00 36.00 11.80 Decline 24.20

How to read: each row is one transaction with a fraud score of 10%. The columns give the expected cost of each action.

So what: with the same score, the cheapest action is different for the two amounts. A review saves more on the large transaction.

Without a review, the cheapest action is to approve the $50 transaction and to decline the $1,000 transaction. A review decreases the expected cost by $24.20 for the large transaction and by $2.70 for the small one. Thus the amount changes the action, not only the score. Section 5d uses this result.

Technical note. For a transaction with amount \(a\) and fraud score \(p\), the expected cost of each action is:

Action Expected cost Actual cost with the label \(y\)
Approve \(p \cdot a \cdot L\) \(y \cdot a \cdot L\)
Decline \((1-p)(m \cdot a + f)\) \((1-y)(m \cdot a + f)\)
Review \(p \cdot a \cdot L (1-q) + (1-p) f_r\) \(y \cdot a \cdot L (1-q) + (1-y) f_r\)

The symbols and their values are:

  • \(L\): the loss share, 100% of the amount (as-01).
  • \(m\) and \(f\): the costs of a false decline, 3% of the amount and $10 (as-02).
  • \(q\): the catch rate of a review, 90% (as-05).
  • \(f_r\): the friction cost of a review for a good customer, $2 (as-05).

The functions expected_costs() and actual_cost() in case02_helpers.py apply these formulas. The total cost of a policy is the sum of the actual costs. It has three parts: fraud loss, false decline cost and review friction. The function summary() gives each part for each month.

All policies in this step use the same review capacity: 3 analysts × 40 alerts = 120 alerts each day (as-03). A real-time decision cannot wait for the end of the day. Thus the policy uses a threshold, not a daily list of the alerts. The code sets the threshold on month 4, so that the mean number of alerts each day equals the capacity (threshold_for_capacity()).

5c. Action tiers

How many actions does the policy have?

Why this question matters. Each extra action costs money to run, but it can decrease the total cost. The number of actions sets if the merchant needs an analyst team, and how large.

Ways to do it. The split axis is the number of actions that the policy can take on a transaction. The answers are one, two, three, or more than three actions.

Actions Method Advantage Main risk Status
One Approve all transactions No model and no team. The merchant pays all fraud. Reference: the baseline of Step 2e
Two Approve or decline, with one threshold on the score Simple. No analyst team. Each transaction with a medium score gets a bad choice: approve and accept the fraud, or decline and lose a good customer. Test it
Three Approve, review or decline, with the review capacity as a limit The analysts stop the fraud in the medium scores and release the good customers. It needs an analyst team. The capacity limits the review tier. Test it
More than three Add a step-up check, for example a one-time code to the card holder (3-D Secure) A cheap check for a medium score. The data has no result of a step-up check. We cannot measure its catch rate or its friction. Screened out: no data. A next step.

Evidence. All options use the GBM score after the recalibration. The code sets the thresholds of each option on month 4 to minimize the total cost, and gives the result on months 5–6. Two tiers use one threshold on the score. Three tiers use a decline threshold on the score, and the next highest scores fill the review capacity.

Evidence: approve all, two tiers and three tiers, months 5–6 
# Purpose: Compare one, two and three actions on months 5–6 (dec-05).
# Input:   `p_valid`, `p_test`, `valid`, `test`, `fit_policy()`, `apply_policy()`, `summary()`.
# Output:  `pol_2`, `pol_3` (policy rules), table `dec05`.

pol_2 = fit_policy("prob2", p_valid, valid)
pol_3 = fit_policy("prob3", p_valid, valid)
dec05 = pd.DataFrame([
    {"Option": "Reference: approve all", **summary(test, np.zeros(len(test), int))},
    {"Option": "A. Two tiers", **summary(test, apply_policy(pol_2, p_test, test))},
    {"Option": "B. Three tiers", **summary(test, apply_policy(pol_3, p_test, test))},
]).set_index("Option")
saving = dec05.iloc[1]["Total cost ($/month)"] - dec05.iloc[2]["Total cost ($/month)"]
team = COST["analysts"] * COST["analyst_day"] * 30
N.update({"d5_all": f"${dec05.iloc[0]['Total cost ($/month)']:,.0f}",
          "d5_two": f"${dec05.iloc[1]['Total cost ($/month)']:,.0f}",
          "d5_saving": f"${saving:,.0f}", "d5_team": f"${team:,.0f}",
          "d5_vs_team": "more than" if saving > team else "less than",
          "d5_fdr_a": f"{dec05.iloc[1]['Decline rate of good transactions']:.2%}",
          "d5_fdr_b": f"{dec05.iloc[2]['Decline rate of good transactions']:.2%}"})
fmt(dec05, SUM_FMT)
Fraud loss ($/month) False decline cost ($/month) Review friction ($/month) Total cost ($/month) Fraud $ stopped Decline rate of good transactions Alerts each day (mean) Days over capacity
Option
Reference: approve all 470,983 0 0 470,983 0.0% 0.00% 0 0%
A. Two tiers 199,068 69,970 0 269,039 57.7% 5.47% 0 0%
B. Three tiers 168,320 63,440 5,126 236,886 64.3% 4.95% 92 5%

How to read: each row is one policy on months 5–6. The cost columns are dollars each month. The last two columns show the use of the review capacity.

So what: the review tier decreases the total cost and the decline rate of good transactions at the same time.

Decision. Three tiers: approve, review or decline, with the review capacity as a limit.

Why. Approve all costs $470,983 each month, and two tiers cost $269,039. The three tiers decrease the total cost by a further $32,153 each month. This is more than the cost of the analyst team, $27,000 each month (as-03, as-04).

The decline rate of good transactions goes from 5.47% to 4.95%. The review tier does the work that a single threshold cannot do: it separates fraud from good customers in the medium scores.

What would change the decision. If the decrease of the total cost is less than the cost of the team, use two tiers. This happens if the catch rate of a review (as-05) is low or if the false decline cost (as-02) is low.

5d. The value that puts the transactions in order

Section 5c fixed three tiers. Section 5b showed that the same score can give a different cheapest action for a different amount. Thus the last question of this step is: which value puts the transactions in order for the decline tier and the review tier?

Which value puts the transactions in order for the policy?

Why this question matters. The review capacity does not change. Each alert on a small transaction takes the place of an alert on a large one. The value that puts the transactions in order decides which fraud dollars the analysts can stop.

Ways to do it. The split axis is what the value measures: how likely the fraud is, how much money is at stake, or both.

What the value measures Method Advantage Main risk Status
How likely the fraud is A. The fraud score (probability). Thresholds on the score. Simple. The same threshold for all transactions. Easy to explain to fraud operations. A $5 transaction and a $2,000 transaction with the same score get the same action. Test it
How much money is at stake The amount only. Review the largest amounts first. Simple. It protects the large amounts. It ignores the score. Most large transactions are good, so the analysts examine good customers. Screened out: it does not use the score
Both B. The expected cost in dollars: the cheapest action for each transaction. Review the transactions where a review decreases the expected cost most. It minimizes the total cost directly. It sends the large risky transactions to review first. It needs a correct level of the score (dec-04). The threshold changes with the amount, so a customer can ask “why me?”. Test it

Evidence. Both options use three tiers, the same score and the same review capacity. The code sets them on month 4 and gives the result on months 5–6.

Evidence: thresholds on the score against the expected cost, months 5–6 
# Purpose: Compare the fraud score and the expected cost as the value of the policy (dec-06).
# Input:   `pol_3`, `p_valid`, `p_test`, `valid`, `test`.
# Output:  `pol_usd` (the challenger policy rule), `act_test` (its action on months 5–6), table `dec06`.

pol_usd = fit_policy("dollar", p_valid, valid)
act_test = apply_policy(pol_usd, p_test, test)
dec06 = pd.DataFrame([
    {"Option": "A. Fraud score", **summary(test, apply_policy(pol_3, p_test, test))},
    {"Option": "B. Expected cost", **summary(test, act_test)},
]).set_index("Option")
saving6 = dec06.iloc[0]["Total cost ($/month)"] - dec06.iloc[1]["Total cost ($/month)"]
N.update({"d6_saving": f"${saving6:,.0f}",
          "d6_stop_a": f"{dec06.iloc[0]['Fraud $ stopped']:.1%}",
          "d6_stop_b": f"{dec06.iloc[1]['Fraud $ stopped']:.1%}",
          "d6_fdr_b": f"{dec06.iloc[1]['Decline rate of good transactions']:.2%}",
          "d6_cost_b": f"${dec06.iloc[1]['Total cost ($/month)']:,.0f}",
          "d6_over": f"{dec06.iloc[1]['Days over capacity']:.0%}"})

Fraud loss ($/month) False decline cost ($/month) Review friction ($/month) Total cost ($/month) Fraud $ stopped Decline rate of good transactions Alerts each day (mean) Days over capacity
Option
A. Fraud score 168,320 63,440 5,126 236,886 64.3% 4.95% 92 5%
B. Expected cost 135,768 31,933 4,911 172,612 71.2% 2.46% 90 5%

How to read: each row is one policy with three tiers on months 5–6. Both rows use the same score and the same review capacity.

So what: the expected cost stops more fraud dollars and costs less each month than thresholds on the score.

Decision. The expected cost in dollars. This policy is the challenger.

Why. The expected cost decreases the total cost by $64,274 each month against the fraud score. It stops 71.2% of the fraud dollars, against 64.3%.

A fraud score shows how likely a fraud is. The expected cost shows how much money is at risk. The business decision is about money, so the expected cost is the correct value. On 5% of the test days, the alerts are more than the capacity. Fraud operations can move these alerts to the next day or decline the lowest ones.

What would change the decision. Assume that the false decline cost does not change with the amount. Also assume that fraud amounts are like good amounts. Then the two options give the same result, and option A is simpler.

Business note. Each transaction now has a score at the level of the recent fraud rate and one action. The challenger policy approves, reviews or declines by the expected cost in dollars, inside the capacity of 120 alerts each day. On months 5–6, it costs $172,612 each month and stops 71.2% of the fraud dollars. It declines 2.46% of the good transactions. Step 6 checks the challenger against the champion with the five branches of the evaluation framework.

Step 6. Evaluate

Step 5 changed the fraud score into a policy. Each transaction gets one action from its expected cost, inside the review capacity. Now we must judge this challenger policy as a whole. This step uses the five branches of the evaluation framework of Step 3a, one at a time. We keep the rules of Step 3a, also when a result fails a rule.

Purpose. This step answers: is the challenger good enough for a test, in model metrics and in dollars? It supports this decision: approve the challenger policy for the champion/challenger test.

All results in this step use the test months 5–6. The model, the recalibration and the thresholds never saw these months. The table below repeats the five rules of Step 3a. We set them before the evidence, and we do not change them here.

Branch Question Rule
1. Order of risk Does the score put fraud above good transactions better than the champion? The PR-AUC and the dollar recall in the top 2% are both above the champion. The GBM is 10% or more above the logistic regression on month 4.
2. Level Is the mean score equal to the actual fraud rate? A difference of less than 0.5 points.
3. Stability Does the score keep its power after the training months? A PSI of less than 0.1, and a PR-AUC on months 5–6 of 80% or more of month 4.
4. Business value Does the policy decrease the total cost at the same review capacity? A lower total cost, and a decline rate of good transactions of 3% or less (as-08).
5. Explainability Can fraud operations read why the policy declines? The leaves with a decline rate of 50% or more hold 50% or more of all declines.

6a. Branch 1: order of risk

The question: does the challenger score put fraud above good transactions better than the champion? The champion score is the fraud rate of its rule segment (as-06). The challenger score is the GBM score after the recalibration. The rule has two parts:

  • On months 5–6, the PR-AUC and the dollar recall in the top 2% of scores are both above the champion.
  • The model rule of Step 4b: the GBM replaces the logistic regression only if its PR-AUC on month 4 is 10% or more higher (relative).
Branch 1: PR-AUC and dollar recall of the champion and the challenger, and the model rule on month 4 
# Purpose: Measure branch 1 (order of risk) on months 5–6, and the model rule of dec-03 on month 4.
# Input:   `test`, `valid`, `champ_score()`, `p_test`, `score_valid`, `score_valid_lr`, `score_metrics()`.
# Output:  Table `eval_order`, `champ_test` (champion score, months 5–6), `lr_gain`.

# The setup cell imports chart_style as `cs`. This guard keeps the part usable with an older setup cell.
if "cs" not in globals():
    import chart_style as cs
    cs.setup()

# Rules of the evaluation framework (Step 3a, set before the evidence). Fallback: the same values from the brief.
RULES = globals().get("RULES", {"b1_model_gain": 0.10, "b2_level_gap": 0.005, "b3_psi": 0.10, "b3_pr_keep": 0.80,
                                 "b4_fdr": 0.03, "b5_leaf_rate": 0.50, "b5_leaf_share": 0.50})

champ_test = champ_score(test)
eval_order = pd.DataFrame([
    {"Score": "Champion: static rules (as-06)", **score_metrics(test, champ_test)},
    {"Score": "Challenger: GBM after the recalibration", **score_metrics(test, p_test)},
]).set_index("Score")
m_champ, m_chal = eval_order.iloc[0], eval_order.iloc[1]

# Model rule (dec-03): relative PR-AUC gain of the GBM over the logistic regression on month 4.
pr4_gbm = average_precision_score(valid["isFraud"], score_valid)
pr4_lr = average_precision_score(valid["isFraud"], score_valid_lr)
lr_gain = pr4_gbm / pr4_lr - 1

b1_pass = (m_chal["PR-AUC"] > m_champ["PR-AUC"]
           and m_chal["Dollar recall, top 2%"] > m_champ["Dollar recall, top 2%"] and lr_gain >= RULES["b1_model_gain"])
N.update({
    "e1_pr_champ": f"{m_champ['PR-AUC']:.3f}", "e1_pr_chal": f"{m_chal['PR-AUC']:.3f}",
    "e1_usd_champ": f"{m_champ['Dollar recall, top 2%']:.1%}",
    "e1_usd_chal": f"{m_chal['Dollar recall, top 2%']:.1%}",
    "e1_pr4_gbm": f"{pr4_gbm:.3f}", "e1_pr4_lr": f"{pr4_lr:.3f}", "e1_lr_gain": f"{lr_gain:+.0%}",
    "b1_verdict": "The challenger passes branch 1." if b1_pass else "The challenger fails branch 1.",
})
fmt(eval_order, METRIC_FMT)

On months 5–6, the challenger has a PR-AUC of 0.486, against 0.269 for the champion. In the top 2% of scores, the challenger finds 26.5% of the fraud dollars. The champion finds 17.0%.

On month 4, the GBM has a PR-AUC of 0.574, and the logistic regression has 0.329. The relative gain is +75%, against the limit of +10%. The challenger passes branch 1.

6b. Branch 2: level

The question: is the mean score equal to the actual fraud rate, on months that the recalibration did not use? The policy multiplies the score by the amount (Step 5b). Thus a score that is too high declines too many good customers, and a score that is too low approves too much fraud. The recalibration of Step 5a used month 4. The table checks months 5 and 6.

Branch 2: mean score after the recalibration against the actual fraud rate, months 5–6 
# Purpose: Measure branch 2 (level): mean score against the actual fraud rate on the test months.
# Input:   `test`, `p_test` (score after the recalibration of dec-04).
# Output:  Table `level`, `level_gap` (mean score minus the actual fraud rate, months 5–6).

level = (pd.DataFrame({"Month": test["month"].to_numpy(), "Actual fraud rate": test["isFraud"].to_numpy(),
                       "Mean score": p_test})
         .groupby("Month").mean())
level.index = [f"Month {m}" for m in level.index]
level.loc["Months 5–6"] = [test["isFraud"].mean(), p_test.mean()]
level["Difference (points)"] = (level["Mean score"] - level["Actual fraud rate"]) * 100
level_gap = p_test.mean() - test["isFraud"].mean()

b2_pass = abs(level_gap) < RULES["b2_level_gap"]
N.update({"e2_mean": f"{p_test.mean():.2%}", "e2_actual": f"{test['isFraud'].mean():.2%}",
          "e2_gap": f"{level_gap * 100:+.2f}",
          "b2_verdict": "The challenger passes branch 2." if b2_pass else "The challenger fails branch 2."})
fmt(level, {"Actual fraud rate": "{:.2%}", "Mean score": "{:.2%}", "Difference (points)": "{:+.2f}"})
Actual fraud rate Mean score Difference (points)
Month 5 3.47% 3.32% -0.15
Month 6 3.47% 3.50% +0.03
Months 5–6 3.47% 3.41% -0.06

On months 5–6, the mean score is 3.41%, and the actual fraud rate is 3.47%. The difference is -0.06 points, against the limit of 0.5 points. The challenger passes branch 2. The expected cost of Step 5b can use this score.

6c. Branch 3: stability

The question: does the score keep its power after the training months? Two metrics answer it, because they find different types of drift:

  • PSI of the score. It compares the score distribution of month 6 with months 1–3. It finds a change of the population. It needs no label.
  • PR-AUC over time. It compares the PR-AUC on months 5–6 with the PR-AUC on month 4. It finds a change of the fraud patterns. It needs the label.

The code uses the same model m_b as Step 3c. It does not train a new model. The recalibration does not change the order of the scores, so it does not change the PSI or the PR-AUC.

Branch 3: PSI of the score (month 6 against months 1–3) and PR-AUC by month 
# Purpose: Measure branch 3 (stability): PSI of the score and the PR-AUC of each month after training.
# Input:   `m_b`, `train`, `valid`, `test`, `p_valid`, `p_test`, `DELTA`, `psi()`, `pr4_gbm`.
# Output:  `score_train` (GBM score of months 1–3, Part 2 uses it too), table `stab`, `psi_score6`, `pr_ratio`.

# Score of the training months, with the same recalibration as the test months.
score_train = predict(m_b, train)
p_train = shift_logodds(score_train, DELTA)
m6 = (test["month"] == 6).to_numpy()
m5 = (test["month"] == 5).to_numpy()
psi_score6 = psi(p_train, p_test[m6])

# PR-AUC of each month. Month 4 is the reference: the model never saw it, but it is next to training.
pr_month = {4: pr4_gbm,
            5: average_precision_score(test["isFraud"][m5], p_test[m5]),
            6: average_precision_score(test["isFraud"][m6], p_test[m6])}
pr56 = average_precision_score(test["isFraud"], p_test)
pr_ratio = pr56 / pr4_gbm

stab = pd.DataFrame([
    ("PSI of the score, month 6 against months 1–3", f"{psi_score6:.3f}", "Less than 0.1"),
    ("PR-AUC, month 4 (reference)", f"{pr_month[4]:.3f}", ""),
    ("PR-AUC, month 5", f"{pr_month[5]:.3f}", ""),
    ("PR-AUC, month 6", f"{pr_month[6]:.3f}", ""),
    ("PR-AUC, months 5–6", f"{pr56:.3f}", ""),
    ("PR-AUC of months 5–6 as a share of month 4", f"{pr_ratio:.0%}", "80% or more"),
], columns=["Metric", "Result", "Rule"]).set_index("Metric")

b3_pass = psi_score6 < RULES["b3_psi"] and pr_ratio >= RULES["b3_pr_keep"]
N.update({"e3_psi": f"{psi_score6:.3f}", "e3_pr4": f"{pr_month[4]:.3f}", "e3_pr56": f"{pr56:.3f}",
          "e3_ratio": f"{pr_ratio:.0%}", "e3_drop": f"{1 - pr_ratio:.0%}",
          "b3_verdict": "The challenger passes branch 3." if b3_pass else "The challenger fails branch 3."})

The PSI of the score in month 6 is 0.008, far below the limit of 0.1. The population of transactions stays the same. But the PR-AUC goes from 0.574 on month 4 to 0.486 on months 5–6. Thus the score keeps 85% of its power, against the limit of 80%. The challenger passes branch 3.

The two metrics tell different stories. The PSI says “no drift”, but the score loses 15% of its PR-AUC. The fraud patterns change, and the PSI cannot see this change. Thus a PSI alone is not a safe check in production. Part 2 uses this result for the retrain decision.

6d. Branch 4: business value

The question: at the same review capacity, does the challenger decrease the total cost against the champion? This is the main business test. Both policies have the same three tiers and the same capacity of 120 alerts each day (as-03). Only the score and the value that ranks the transactions change:

  • Champion (as-06). The rules of a decision tree with 3 levels, fit on month 1. The code sets its decline and review thresholds on month 4, with the method of Step 5c.
  • Challenger. The GBM score after the recalibration, and the expected cost in dollars (Step 5d).

The guardrail is the decline rate of good transactions. A decline of a good customer has a cost in the model (as-02), but it also hurts the brand. Thus the rule adds a hard limit of 3% (as-08). Marketing must confirm this limit before the test.

How much of the gain depends on the champion?

The champion is our assumption (as-06, Step 0b). A weak champion makes any challenger look good. Thus we repeat branch 4 against four champions, from weak to strong. Each champion uses the same three tiers, the same review capacity and the same method to set its thresholds on month 4 (Step 5c). Only its score changes:

Champion Score Why it is in the ladder

3. Simple model Logistic regression of Step 4b, fit on months 1–3 A team with a model, but with a simple model.
4. Same model, score thresholds The GBM of the challenger, ranked by the fraud score (Step 5d, option A) The strongest champion: the same score as the challenger. Only the dollar order is missing.
Branch 4 again: the challenger against four champions, from weak to strong (months 5–6) 
# Purpose: Show how much of the saving of branch 4 depends on the champion assumption (as-06).
# Input:   `train`, `valid`, `test`, `act_champ`, `act_test`, `lr`, `lr_cols`, `pol_3`, `p_test`,
#          `encode()`, `fit_policy()`, `apply_policy()`, `summary()`.
# Output:  Table `ladder`, N values `lad_*`, a bar chart of the saving against each champion.

def tree_champion(fit_frame, depth):
    """A rule champion: a decision tree on the numeric features. Its leaf fraud rate is the score."""
    X_fit = encode(fit_frame, fit_frame, NUM_COLS, []).fillna(-999)
    tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth, min_samples_leaf=200, random_state=SEED)
    tree.fit(X_fit, fit_frame["isFraud"])
    score = lambda f: tree.predict_proba(encode(f, fit_frame, NUM_COLS, []).fillna(-999))[:, 1]
    return score(valid), score(test)


def champion_actions(s_valid, s_test):
    """Thresholds on the score, set on month 4 with the capacity limit (Step 5c), then applied to months 5-6."""
    return apply_policy(fit_policy("prob3", s_valid, valid), s_test, test)


as_obj = {c: object for c in CAT_COLS}
s5_valid, s5_test = tree_champion(train, depth=5)
lr_test = lr.predict_proba(test[lr_cols].astype(as_obj))[:, 1]
lr_valid = lr.predict_proba(valid[lr_cols].astype(as_obj))[:, 1]
champions = {
    "1. Static rules (as-06)": act_champ,
    "2. Rules from more data": champion_actions(s5_valid, s5_test),
    "3. Simple model": champion_actions(lr_valid, lr_test),
    "4. Same model, score thresholds": apply_policy(pol_3, p_test, test),
}
cost_chal = summary(test, act_test)["Total cost ($/month)"]
rows = []
for name, act in champions.items():
    s = summary(test, act)
    rows.append({"Champion": name, "Total cost ($/month)": s["Total cost ($/month)"],
                 "Fraud $ stopped": s["Fraud $ stopped"],
                 "Decline rate of good transactions": s["Decline rate of good transactions"],

6e. Branch 5: explainability

The question: can fraud operations read why the policy declines a transaction? The GBM gives no rules. Fraud operations and the partners ask “why did you decline this transaction?”. A fraud decline needs no adverse action notice, unlike a credit decline. Thus the law does not ask for a reason for each decline. But the rule of Step 3a still applies, because fraud operations must understand and check the declines.

The method is a surrogate tree. It is a small decision tree that copies the decline decisions of the challenger. The tree has these parameters:

  • 3 levels, so that each rule has three conditions or fewer.
  • 500 transactions or more in each leaf, so that each rule covers a real segment.
  • Only features that people can read. These are the amount, the hour, the distance, the email match, the identity flag and the history features. Four fields of the card, the product and the device complete the list.

The rule of branch 5: the leaves with a decline rate of 50% or more must hold 50% or more of all declines. If this is true, a few readable rules explain most declines.

Branch 5: surrogate tree with readable rules for the decline tier 
# Purpose: Fit a surrogate tree with 3 levels on the decline decision of the challenger (branch 5).
# Input:   `test`, `act_test`, `CAT_COLS`, `SEED`.
# Output:  `sur` (the tree), table `leaves`, `leaf_rules()`, `sur_share` (share of declines in leaves of 50%+).

READ_COLS = ["TransactionAmt", "hour", "dist1", "email_match", "has_identity",
             "uid_n", "uid_amt_ratio", "uid_n_today", "card_n_today"]
READ_CAT = [c for c in ["ProductCD", "card4", "card6", "DeviceType"] if c in CAT_COLS]
X_read = pd.get_dummies(test[READ_COLS + READ_CAT], columns=READ_CAT, dtype=float)
X_read["uid_hours_since"] = test["uid_hours_since"].fillna(10_000)  # 10,000 = no earlier transaction
X_read = X_read.fillna(-1)
is_decline = (act_test == 2).astype(int)
sur = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=500, random_state=SEED)
sur.fit(X_read, is_decline)


def leaf_rules(tree, names, binary):
    """Return the rule text of each leaf of a fitted tree."""
    t, rules = tree.tree_, {}

    def walk(node, conds):
        if t.children_left[node] == -1:
            rules[node] = " and ".join(conds)
            return
        f, thr = names[t.feature[node]], t.threshold[node]
        left, right = ((f"{f} = 0", f"{f} = 1") if f in binary
                       else (f"{f} ≤ {thr:,.1f}", f"{f} > {thr:,.1f}"))
        walk(t.children_left[node], conds + [left])
        walk(t.children_right[node], conds + [right])

    walk(0, [])
    return rules


binary = {c for c in X_read.columns if set(X_read[c].unique()) <= {0.0, 1.0}}
rules = leaf_rules(sur, list(X_read.columns), binary)
leaves = (pd.DataFrame({"leaf": sur.apply(X_read), "decline": is_decline})
          .groupby("leaf")["decline"].agg(["size", "mean", "sum"]))
leaves.columns = ["Transactions", "Decline rate", "Declines"]
leaves["Share of all declines"] = leaves["Declines"] / is_decline.sum()
leaves.insert(0, "Rule", leaves.index.map(rules))
leaves = leaves.sort_values("Decline rate", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

# Rule of branch 5: share of all declines in the leaves with a decline rate of 50% or more.
sur_share = leaves.loc[leaves["Decline rate"] >= RULES["b5_leaf_rate"], "Share of all declines"].sum()
top = leaves.iloc[0]
b5_pass = sur_share >= RULES["b5_leaf_share"]
N.update({"sur_rule": top["Rule"], "sur_rate": f"{top['Decline rate']:.0%}",
          "sur_share": f"{top['Share of all declines']:.0%}",
          "sur_all": f"{is_decline.mean():.1%}",
          "sur_n_big": f"{(leaves['Decline rate'] >= RULES['b5_leaf_rate']).sum()}",
          "sur_big_share": f"{sur_share:.0%}",
          "b5_verdict": "The challenger passes branch 5." if b5_pass else "The challenger fails branch 5."})
fmt(leaves.drop(columns="Declines"),
    {"Transactions": "{:,.0f}", "Decline rate": "{:.1%}", "Share of all declines": "{:.0%}"})

Three levels of readable rules cannot copy the score. The GBM declines a transaction because of many small signals together, and a rule with three conditions cannot show them. The rules still show the main patterns, and fraud operations can use them to find new fraud patterns. They cannot replace the score. Step 7 adds a control for this gap.

The challenger passes 4 of the 5 branches. The branches that fail are: explainability.

What a failure means for the test:

  • Explainability (branch 5). The policy cannot give a short readable rule for most declines. Fraud operations can still use the rules to find patterns, and a decline needs no adverse action notice. Thus this failure does not stop a test. But a partner or a regulator can ask for a reason for each decline. Then a decline reason must come from another method, and Step 4b gives the alternative.
  • Any other branch. A failure of branches 1 to 4 goes back to the owner of the decision before the test. The test plan of Step 7 assumes that branches 1 to 4 pass.

Business note. The challenger passes 4 of the 5 branches of the evaluation framework. At the same review capacity, it decreases the total cost by $126,820 each month (42%). It declines 2.46% of good transactions, inside the guardrail of 3%.

Two results need attention. The score loses 15% of its PR-AUC after month 4, and the PSI does not show this loss. Three levels of readable rules do not explain most declines. Step 7 changes the result into a test plan, and Part 2 sets the retrain schedule.

Step 7. Implementation

Step 6 showed that the challenger passes 4 of the 5 branches. At the same review capacity, it decreases the total cost by $126,820 each month on the test months. A result on past data is not yet a decision.

This step answers three questions. Is the analyst team the correct size? Does the result hold for other costs? How do we test the policy safely?

Purpose. This step changes the evaluation into a team size, a range of dollar results and a test plan. It supports this decision: go or no-go for a champion/challenger test on 10% of transactions.

7a. Value of one more analyst

The review capacity is a limit of the policy (as-03). Each analyst examines 40 alerts each day and costs $9,000 each month (as-04). One more analyst lets the policy send more transactions to review. The question: does the decrease of the total cost pay for the analyst?

The code repeats the challenger policy for 0 to 6 analysts. For each team size, it sets the thresholds again on month 4 and measures the total cost on months 5–6. The team cost is separate from the total cost (glossary), so the chart adds them.

Total cost for 0 to 6 analysts, and the shadow price of one more analyst 
# Purpose: Find the value of one more analyst (as-03, as-04): the shadow price of the review capacity.
# Input:   `COST`, `fit_policy()`, `apply_policy()`, `summary()`, `p_valid`, `valid`, `p_test`, `test`.
# Output:  Table `cap`, `best` (team size with the lowest total cost + team cost).

rows = []
for n_an in range(0, 7):
    c = {**COST, "analysts": n_an}
    # Set the thresholds again on month 4 for this capacity. Then measure on months 5–6.
    rule = fit_policy("dollar", p_valid, valid, c)
    s = summary(test, apply_policy(rule, p_test, test), c)
    rows.append({"Analysts": n_an, "Alerts each day": capacity(c),
                 "Total cost ($/month)": s["Total cost ($/month)"],
                 "Team cost ($/month)": n_an * COST["analyst_day"] * 30})
cap = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Analysts")
cap["Cost + team ($/month)"] = cap["Total cost ($/month)"] + cap["Team cost ($/month)"]
cap["Saving from the last analyst ($/month)"] = -cap["Total cost ($/month)"].diff()
best = int(cap["Cost + team ($/month)"].idxmin())
N.update({"cap_best": str(best), "cap_now": str(COST["analysts"]),
          "cap_next": f"${cap.loc[COST['analysts'] + 1, 'Saving from the last analyst ($/month)']:,.0f}",
          "analyst_month": f"${COST['analyst_day'] * 30:,.0f}",
          "cap_gap": f"${cap.loc[COST['analysts'], 'Cost + team ($/month)'] - cap.loc[best, 'Cost + team ($/month)']:,.0f}"})

7c. Rollout plan

The result of Step 6 comes from past transactions. Fraud patterns, customers and costs change. A controlled test gives the proof before a full rollout. The plan has five parts.

1. Test design. Send a random 10% of transactions to the challenger. The other 90% stay with the champion. A random allocation makes the two arms equal in all other ways, so the difference comes from the policy.

Each arm gets the same share of the review capacity as of the transactions. Thus the challenger arm gets 10% of the alerts each day, and the test keeps the condition “same review capacity”.

The test must run long enough to find the difference in cost. The code estimates the number of days from the cost of each transaction on months 5–6. It uses a significance level of 5% (two-sided) and a power of 80%.

Technical note. Let d be the difference of the mean cost for each transaction (champion minus challenger). Let s₁² and s₂² be the variances of the cost for each transaction under the champion and the challenger. Let v be the transactions each day, and w the share of the challenger arm. Then the test needs D days: D = (1.96 + 0.84)² × (s₁² / (1 − w) + s₂² / w) / (v × d²).

This formula uses a normal approximation. The cost of a fraud transaction has a long tail, so we double D for safety. The fraud label also arrives late (as-07), so the result needs time after the last day of the test.

Test design: volume of each arm and the number of days to find the difference in cost 
# Purpose: Size the champion/challenger test on 10% of transactions (7c).
# Input:   `test`, `act_champ`, `act_test`, `actual_cost()`, `COST`, `capacity()`.
# Output:  Table `rollout`, `test_days`.

TEST_SHARE = globals().get("TEST_SHARE", 0.10)  # Share of transactions in the challenger arm (setup cell)
Z = 1.96 + 0.84     # Significance 5% (two-sided) and power 80%

cost_ch = actual_cost(test, act_champ)
cost_cl = actual_cost(test, act_test)
per_day = len(test) / test["day"].nunique()
diff = cost_ch.mean() - cost_cl.mean()
days_raw = Z ** 2 * (cost_ch.var() / (1 - TEST_SHARE) + cost_cl.var() / TEST_SHARE) / (per_day * diff ** 2)
test_days = int(np.ceil(2 * days_raw))  # Double the estimate: the cost has a long tail.

rollout = pd.DataFrame({"Value": [
    f"{per_day:,.0f}", f"{per_day * TEST_SHARE:,.0f}", f"{per_day * TEST_SHARE * test['isFraud'].mean():,.0f}",
    f"{capacity() * TEST_SHARE:,.0f}", f"${diff:,.2f}", f"{days_raw:,.1f}", f"{test_days}",
]}, index=["Transactions each day (months 5–6)", "Transactions each day, challenger arm",
           "Fraud transactions each day, challenger arm", "Alerts each day, challenger arm",
           "Difference of the mean cost for each transaction", "Days to find the difference (formula)",
           "Days to find the difference (doubled)"])
N.update({"ro_arm_day": f"{per_day * TEST_SHARE:,.0f}", "ro_alerts": f"{capacity() * TEST_SHARE:,.0f}",
          "ro_days": f"{test_days}", "ro_diff": f"${diff:,.2f}"})
rollout
Value
Transactions each day (months 5–6) 2,856
Transactions each day, challenger arm 286
Fraud transactions each day, challenger arm 10
Alerts each day, challenger arm 12
Difference of the mean cost for each transaction $1.48
Days to find the difference (formula) 7.7
Days to find the difference (doubled) 16

The challenger arm gets about 286 transactions and 12 alerts each day. The challenger saves $1.48 for each transaction. To find this difference, the test needs about 16 days of transactions. Then it needs time for the chargebacks. The data has no chargeback dates, so Fraud Operations must give this delay.

2. Main KPI. The total cost for each 1,000 transactions in each arm, after the chargeback delay. The total cost includes the fraud loss, the false declines and the review friction (Step 5b). The cost for each 1,000 transactions makes the two arms of different size comparable.

3. Guardrails. Check these values each week:

  • The decline rate of good transactions of the challenger arm: 3% or less (as-08). The label arrives late, so the decline rate of all transactions is the early signal.
  • The alerts each day against the capacity of the arm.
  • The PSI of the score against months 1–3, and the PR-AUC of each month with labels (Part 2).

4. Kill criteria. Stop the test in any of these cases:

  • The decline rate of all transactions in the challenger arm is above 3% for two weeks in a row.
  • The fraud loss for each 1,000 transactions of the challenger arm is above the champion arm for one full month with labels.
  • The PSI of the score is more than 0.25.

5. Top risks.

Risk Effect Control
The cost of a false decline (as-02) is higher than the assumption. The challenger declines too many good customers. The decrease of the total cost is too high. Finance and Marketing confirm as-02 and as-08 before the test. The guardrail and the kill criteria stop the test.
The fraud patterns change after the training months. The score loses power, but the PSI stays low (Step 6c). Retrain each month (Part 2). Check the PR-AUC of each month with labels.
Fraud operations cannot read why the policy declines (branch 5). A partner complaint has no short answer. Fraud operations cannot check the declines. Give the surrogate rules to fraud operations as patterns, not as reasons. If a partner asks for reasons, use the alternative of Step 4b.
The champion is an assumption (as-06). The real champion can be stronger or weaker. The decrease of the total cost changes. The test measures the real champion, because the 90% arm uses it.
The labels arrive late (as-07). The test result and each retrain use labels that are not complete. Read the KPI only after the chargeback delay. Train on all months except the last one when the labels are late.

Decision at the end. If the challenger arm has a lower total cost for each 1,000 transactions and stays inside the guardrail, roll out the challenger. Increase the share step by step and keep the champion arm as a control.

Business note. At the current capacity, the challenger decreases the total cost by $126,820 each month. In each cost case that we tested, the decrease is at least $53,544. The best team size changes the cost by only $1,534 each month.

The recommendation is a test on 10% of transactions for about 16 days, with the guardrail of 3% (as-08). The test uses one score with no retrain. Part 2 examines how fast this score loses power, and when to retrain it.

Part 2: Drift and retrain

Step 7 gave a test plan for one score, the GBM from months 1–3 with no retrain. But Step 6c showed a problem. The PSI of the score stays low, but the score keeps only 85% of its month 4 PR-AUC on months 5–6. Fraud patterns change, and a static score loses value. Part 2 asks two questions: what changes after the training months, and how often must we retrain the score?

Purpose. This part shows how the data and the score change over time. It supports this decision: the retrain schedule and the checks of the model in production.

Drift: what changes after the training months?

A score can lose value in two ways. The population can change: new customers, new products or new devices. Or the relation between the features and fraud can change: the fraudsters find a new method. The PSI finds only the first type. The PR-AUC of each month with labels finds the second type.

The table gives the PSI of the score and of nine important features for months 4, 5 and 6, against months 1–3. A PSI of less than 0.1 is stable. A PSI of more than 0.25 is a large change.

Drift: PSI of the score and of the top features, months 4–6 against months 1–3 
# Purpose: Measure the drift of the score and of the top features after the training months.
# Input:   `txn`, `train`, `p_train`, `p_valid`, `p_test` (Step 6c), `psi()`.
# Output:  Table `drift` (one row for each month, one column for the score and each feature).

imp_feats = [c for c in ["TransactionAmt", "C1", "C13", "card1", "D1", "D1n", "uid_n",
                         "uid_amt_ratio", "card_n_today"] if c in txn.columns]
# Scores after the recalibration of each month. The recalibration keeps the order, so the PSI does not change.
month_score = {4: p_valid, 5: p_test[(test["month"] == 5).to_numpy()], 6: p_test[(test["month"] == 6).to_numpy()]}
rows = []
for mo in [4, 5, 6]:
    part = txn[txn["month"] == mo]
    row = {"Month": mo, "Score": psi(p_train, month_score[mo])}
    row.update({f: psi(train[f], part[f]) for f in imp_feats})
    rows.append(row)
drift = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Month")
feat6 = drift.drop(columns="Score").loc[6]
N.update({"psi_score_6": f"{drift.loc[6, 'Score']:.3f}",
          "psi_max_feat": feat6.idxmax(), "psi_max_val": f"{feat6.max():.2f}",
          "psi_n_large": f"{(feat6 > 0.25).sum()}",
          "psi_uid_n": f"{drift.loc[6, 'uid_n']:.2f}" if "uid_n" in drift else "n/a"})
drift.round(3)

How to read: each bar is the PSI of one variable in month 6. The dashed lines are the limits 0.1 and 0.25. The blue bar is the score.

So what: the score PSI is 0.008, so the population of scores does not move. But Step 6c showed that the PR-AUC goes down. Thus the PSI cannot find this type of drift, and the checks in production must also use the PR-AUC of each month with labels.

The feature with the largest PSI in month 6 is D1n (2.12). D1n is the first day of the card, a date. Its value moves each month, because new cards come into the data. For this reason, the model does not use it (Step 2).

The PSI of uid_n is 0.22. It goes up, because the history of each customer gets longer. In production, a history window of fixed length (for example 90 days) stops this drift.

Retrain schedule

How often do we retrain the score?

Why this question matters. The score loses 15% of its PR-AUC from month 4 to months 5–6 (Step 6c). A weaker score stops less fraud at the same review capacity. But each new model needs a model risk review, a recalibration and new thresholds. Thus a retrain has a cost, and the schedule must pay for it.

Ways to do it. A schedule has two axes: when the retrain happens, and which months the new model learns from.

When Which months Method Advantage Main risk
Never Months 1–3 A. No retrain One model risk review. Stable decisions. The score loses value when fraud patterns change.
Each month All months with labels B. Retrain each month on all labeled months The score learns new patterns. It keeps rare old patterns. A review for each new model. The last month can have labels that are not complete.
Each month The last three months C. Retrain each month on a window of three months It forgets old patterns faster. A smaller training set. Old patterns can come back.
On a trigger All months with labels Retrain when the PSI is above a limit Few retrains. Step 6c showed that the PSI stays low when the score loses power. Thus the trigger does not fire. We screen it out.
Each day or each week All transactions Online learning It follows the newest patterns. The fraud label arrives weeks later, and each change needs a review. We screen it out.

Evidence. The code scores months 5 and 6 with each of the options A, B and C. Each retrain uses only the months before the scored month. Thus each option sees the same data that production has on that date. The metrics are the PR-AUC and the dollar recall in the top 2%. For month 4, all three options are the same model m_b, because all three train on months 1–3.

Evidence: no retrain, monthly retrain and a sliding window of three months 
# Purpose: Compare three retrain schedules on months 5 and 6 (dec-07).
# Input:   `txn`, `m_b`, `fit_gbm()`, `predict()`, `score_metrics()`, `FEATS`, `CAT_COLS`, `score_valid`.
# Output:  Table `dec07` (option × metric × month, months 5–6), `pr_by_month` (PR-AUC of months 4–6 for the chart).

rows = []
# Month 4: all options use m_b (trained on months 1–3).
r4 = score_metrics(valid, score_valid)
for name in ["A. No retrain", "B. Monthly, all months", "C. Monthly, last 3 months"]:
    rows.append({"Month": 4, "Option": name, "PR-AUC": r4["PR-AUC"],
                 "Dollar recall, top 2%": r4["Dollar recall, top 2%"]})
for mo in [5, 6]:
    part = txn[txn["month"] == mo]
    # Each retrain uses only the months before the scored month.
    m_all = fit_gbm(txn[txn["month"] < mo], FEATS, CAT_COLS)
    m_win = fit_gbm(txn[txn["month"].between(mo - 3, mo - 1)], FEATS, CAT_COLS)
    for name, m in [("A. No retrain", m_b), ("B. Monthly, all months", m_all),
                    ("C. Monthly, last 3 months", m_win)]:
        r = score_metrics(part, predict(m, part))
        rows.append({"Month": mo, "Option": name, "PR-AUC": r["PR-AUC"],
                     "Dollar recall, top 2%": r["Dollar recall, top 2%"]})
long = pd.DataFrame(rows)
pr_by_month = long.pivot(index="Month", columns="Option", values="PR-AUC")
dec07 = long[long["Month"] >= 5].pivot(index="Option", columns="Month")
mean_pr = dec07["PR-AUC"].mean(axis=1)
mean_usd = dec07["Dollar recall, top 2%"].mean(axis=1)
N.update({"d7_a": f"{mean_pr.iloc[0]:.3f}", "d7_b": f"{mean_pr.iloc[1]:.3f}",
          "d7_c": f"{mean_pr.iloc[2]:.3f}",
          "d7_usd_a": f"{mean_usd.iloc[0]:.1%}", "d7_usd_b": f"{mean_usd.iloc[1]:.1%}",
          "d7_gain": f"{mean_pr.iloc[1] / mean_pr.iloc[0] - 1:+.0%}",
          "d7_bc": f"{abs(mean_pr.iloc[2] - mean_pr.iloc[1]):.3f}",
          "d7_ab": f"{mean_pr.iloc[1] - mean_pr.iloc[0]:.3f}"})
dec07.round(3)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
style = {"A. No retrain": (cs.GRAY, 1.6), "B. Monthly, all months": (cs.NAVY, 2.2),

for opt, (color, lw) in style.items():
    y = pr_by_month[opt]
    ax.plot(y.index, y, color=color, lw=lw, marker="o", ms=4)
    # Direct labels at the line end. B and C end near each other, so C moves down.
    dy = {"A. No retrain": 0, "B. Monthly, all months": 7, "C. Monthly, last 3 months": -7}[opt]
    cs.label_end(ax, y.index[-1], y.iloc[-1], opt, color=color, dy=dy, bold=opt.startswith("B"))
# Blue: the month 4 start point, the same model for all options.
ax.plot(4, pr_by_month.iloc[0, 0], "o", color=cs.BLUE, ms=8, zorder=5)
ax.set_xticks([4, 5, 6])
ax.set_xticklabels(["Month 4\n(validation)", "Month 5", "Month 6"])
ax.set_xlim(3.8, 7.4)
ax.set_ylabel("PR-AUC")
cs.action_title(fig, f"A monthly retrain lifts the PR-AUC from {N['d7_a']} to {N['d7_b']}",
                "Each retrain uses only the months before the scored month. In month 4, all three options are the same model.")
plt.show()

How to read: each line is one retrain option. All lines start at the same point in month 4, because all options use the same model there. A higher line finds fraud better.

So what: with no retrain, the PR-AUC goes down after month 4. A monthly retrain keeps more of the power of the score.

Decision. Option B: retrain each month on all months with labels.

Why. The mean PR-AUC on months 5 and 6 is:

  • A. No retrain: 0.487.
  • B. Monthly retrain on all months: 0.576.
  • C. Monthly retrain on the last three months: 0.580.

A retrain adds 0.089 of PR-AUC (+18%). In the top 2% of scores, the dollar recall goes from 27.0% to 37.1%. Options B and C differ by only 0.005. We select option B, because it has more training data and keeps rare fraud patterns from older months. The recalibration (Step 5a) and the thresholds (Step 5c) must follow each retrain.

What would change the decision. If the PR-AUC stays stable for three months, a retrain each quarter is enough. It costs less review work. If the chargebacks come late, the last month has labels that are not complete. Then train on all months except the last one.

The policy result of Step 6d uses option A, the score with no retrain. Thus the decrease of the total cost in Step 6d is a low estimate.

Checks in production

The checks follow from the drift results. The PSI is cheap and fast, but it does not see a change of the fraud patterns. The PR-AUC sees this change, but it needs the labels. Thus the plan uses both.

Frequency Check Limit Action
Each day Alerts each day against the capacity; decline rate of all transactions Capacity of 120 alerts; 3% (as-08) Fraud operations move the extra alerts to the next day. Above the limit for two weeks: stop the challenger.
Each week PSI of the score and of the top features, against the training months 0.1 examine; 0.25 act Above 0.25: examine the change before the next retrain.
Each month PR-AUC and dollar recall of the last month with labels 80% or more of the PR-AUC of the validation month (branch 3) Retrain (dec-07), recalibrate (Step 5a) and set the thresholds again on the last month with labels.
Each month Decline rate of good transactions, with labels 3% or less (as-08) Above the limit: stop the challenger (Step 7c).

Business note. The population of transactions stays stable, but the fraud patterns change fast. With no retrain, the score loses 15% of its PR-AUC in two months. A monthly retrain on all months with labels gives a mean PR-AUC of 0.576, against 0.487 with no retrain. The checks in production must use the PR-AUC of each month, not only the PSI. The conclusion collects the results of all steps.

Conclusion

The notebook started with one question: which approve, review and decline policy gives the lowest total cost of fraud, false declines and reviews? Steps 0 to 7 answered it for the test months. Part 2 then showed how fast the answer gets old.

The answer

The challenger policy gives a lower total cost than the champion. It uses a GBM fraud score and the expected cost in dollars, with the same review capacity. On the test months, it decreases the total cost by $126,820 each month (42%) against our base champion.

Against the strongest champion of the ladder, the decrease is $64,274 each month. The champion is our assumption, so the lower value is the result that we can defend. The decrease is at least $53,544 each month for each cost assumption that we tested. It stops 71.2% of the fraud dollars, against 38.4% for the champion.

The price is more declines of good customers: 2.46% against 0.28%. This rate is inside the guardrail of 3% (as-08). The challenger passes 4 of the 5 branches of the evaluation framework. The branches that fail are: explainability.

Recommendation

  1. Test the challenger policy. Send a random 10% of transactions and 10% of the review capacity to the challenger. Run the test for about 16 days (Step 7c). Stop the test if a kill criterion applies.
  2. Confirm two values before the test. Finance and Marketing confirm the cost of a false decline (as-02) and the guardrail limit of 3% (as-08). These values decide the size of the decline tier (Step 7b).
  3. Retrain the score each month on all months with labels. A monthly retrain lifts the mean PR-AUC from 0.487 to 0.576 (Part 2).
  4. Check the PR-AUC of each month, not only the PSI. The PSI of the score stays at 0.008, but the score loses 15% of its PR-AUC (Step 6c).
  5. Do not change the team size before the test. The lowest sum of the total cost and the team cost is at 4 analysts. It is only $1,534 each month below the current team (Step 7a).

What a reviewer should challenge

These limits can change the result most. Each one has a control.

Limitation Effect on the result Control, or what to do next
The costs are assumptions (as-01 to as-05). The dollar values and the size of the decline tier change. The sensitivity check of Step 7b. Finance and Fraud Operations confirm the values.
The guardrail limit of 3% is an assumption (as-08). A lower limit forces fewer declines and a smaller decrease of the total cost. Marketing confirms the limit before the test. The kill criteria use it.
The champion is an assumption (as-06). We built it because the data has no real rules. The gain of the challenger depends on the champion: $64,274 to $126,820 each month. The ladder of four champions in Step 6d. Both policies use the same review capacity and cost method. The test of Step 7c measures the gain against the real rules.
The surrogate tree does not explain most declines (branch 5). Fraud operations cannot give a short reason for each decline. A fraud decline needs no adverse action notice. If a partner asks for reasons, use the alternative of Step 4b.
The PSI does not find a change of the fraud patterns. A score can lose value with a stable PSI. Check the PR-AUC of each month with labels. Retrain each month (dec-07).
The label includes later transactions of a customer after a chargeback (as-07). The history features can look stronger than in production. History from earlier transactions only (dec-02).
The data does not give the date of the chargeback. The retrain test assumes that all labels are complete. Train on all months except the last one when the labels are late.
The policy result uses the score with no retrain. The decrease of the total cost is a low estimate. Part 2 shows the gain of a monthly retrain.

Other limits have a small effect. The data has no customer ID, so uid is a proxy. Vesta masked most features, so reason codes from the raw features have little meaning. The data is a sample of the payment flow of one merchant, so the dollar values are small. Scale the result with the actual volume. Real-time latency is a task for engineering.

Next steps

  1. Business case deck (6–8 slides): the challenger policy for a champion/challenger test on 10% of transactions.
  2. Confirm the cost assumptions with Finance (as-01, as-02), Fraud Operations (as-03, as-05) and Marketing (as-08).
  3. A one-pager for fraud operations: the review capacity, the value of one more analyst and the surrogate rules as patterns.
  4. Add a feature “earlier chargebacks of the customer” when the chargeback dates are available (dec-02).
  5. Set up the checks in production of Part 2 before the start of the test.

Appendix A: data dictionary

The table gives each column that the notebook uses, then each group of masked columns. Vesta masked the meaning of most columns. The meaning comes from the data description of Vesta on the Kaggle competition page. It also uses the answers of Vesta in the Kaggle discussion. The other parts of the table come from this notebook:

  • Bucket. “Feature” means that the fraud score uses the column. Any other value is the bucket of the funnel in Step 4a: 1. Not known at the decision, 2. No stable risk information, 3. Removed to keep the model small.
  • Rule. The first rule of the funnel that removes the column. A group row counts the columns of the group for each rule.
  • Detail. The evidence for the rule, or the type and the share of empty cells of a feature.
  • Other use. The use of the column outside the fraud score, for example the time order or the customer key.
  • Empty. The share of empty cells in all transactions. For a group row, it is the mean of the loaded columns of the group. A dash means that the code does not load the column.

The first table counts the columns in each bucket. The second table shows the named columns and the engineered features first, then the groups of masked columns.
